items.title: 1. Normal haemostasis: the framework for everything that follows
items.priority: Foundation for the P1 to P5 outcomes in this set
items.body:
> **Teaching sequence:** haemostasis → bleeding assessment → patient blood management → major haemorrhage → components and critical-care transfusion → anticoagulation and VTE → ICU coagulopathy → reactions → special haematology.
>
> **Scope:** all 13 parent LO rows / 19 allocated components in the Set 2 master workbook. Related outcomes shared with other sets are covered **only for their assigned haematological components**.

## 1.1 Why bleeding stops — and why this matters to an anaesthetist

- Blood loss is controlled by a coordinated response from **vessel wall, platelets, coagulation factors and fibrinolysis**.
- The older intrinsic/extrinsic diagrams are useful for interpreting laboratory tests, but actual haemostasis proceeds on cell surfaces: **initiation** by tissue factor, **amplification** on activated platelets and **propagation** through a thrombin burst.
- Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, activates factor XIII to cross-link the clot and further activates platelets.
- A patient can have normal conventional PT/APTT yet bleed from impaired platelets, low fibrinogen, excessive fibrinolysis or surgical disruption.

- **Primary haemostasis** begins with vascular injury, exposure of collagen and von Willebrand factor (vWF), platelet adhesion (GPIb–vWF), platelet activation (ADP, thromboxane A₂, thrombin), and aggregation (GPIIb/IIIa–fibrinogen).
- Failure typically produces mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae, epistaxis and immediate oozing.
- **Secondary haemostasis** stabilises that platelet plug through thrombin generation and fibrin; defects more often cause deep tissue/joint bleeding, delayed postoperative haemorrhage or large haematomas.
- These are patterns, not absolute diagnostic rules.

**Natural anticoagulants limit the response:**

- Antithrombin inhibits thrombin/Xa (potentiated by heparin); activated protein C with protein S inactivates Va/VIIIa; tissue-factor pathway inhibitor restrains tissue-factor–VIIa.
- **Fibrinolysis** converts plasminogen to plasmin through tissue plasminogen activator; plasmin breaks down fibrin (D-dimer when cross-linked).
- PAI-1 and α₂-antiplasmin regulate this system.
- Hyperfibrinolysis can cause rapid clot breakdown after major trauma, obstetric haemorrhage, liver disease or prolonged CPB; indiscriminate antifibrinolysis can be inappropriate when fibrinolysis is already suppressed.

### A useful clinical distinction

| **Pattern** | **Likely processes** | **Important tests** |
|---|---|---|
| Surgical focal bleeding | Vessel, anastomosis, surgical bed | Direct inspection/control; tests can be normal |
| Diffuse microvascular oozing | Dilution/consumption of platelets or fibrinogen, hypothermia, acidosis, DIC, antiplatelet drugs | Platelet count, fibrinogen, PT/APTT, VEM as available |
| Mucosal bleeding/petechiae | Platelet/vWF problems | Count, blood film, medication history, vWF studies if indicated |
| Deep/delayed bleeding | Coagulation factor deficiency, inhibitors, anticoagulants | PT/APTT, fibrinogen, mixing study/factor assays |
| Thrombosis despite bleeding | DIC, HIT, thrombotic microangiopathy, malignancy | Trend, film, fibrinogen, D-dimer, organ injury, targeted tests |

- **Remember:** the patient can be both bleeding and thrombosing. DIC, sepsis-associated coagulopathy, malignancy and HIT all make a simple “bleeding versus clotting” dichotomy misleading.

## 1.2 How to interpret routine coagulation investigations

**Platelet count** detects thrombocytopenia, not platelet function. Poor function occurs with aspirin, P2Y₁₂ inhibitors, uraemia, CPB, inherited disorders and hypothermia despite a normal count. Unexpected very low automated counts should be confirmed on film or an alternative anticoagulant sample to exclude EDTA-related pseudothrombocytopenia.

- **PT/INR** interrogates mainly tissue factor/extrinsic and common-pathway factor activity; useful for warfarin effect, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease and factor deficiencies.
- INR standardisation was designed for warfarin, not as a comprehensive haemostasis index in cirrhosis.
- **APTT** evaluates contact/intrinsic and common pathways; prolonged by UFH, some factor deficiencies, inhibitors and lupus anticoagulant.
- A normal APTT does not exclude a direct Xa inhibitor.
- A prolonged APTT can reflect thrombotic risk with lupus anticoagulant, rather than bleeding.
- **Thrombin time** is highly sensitive to heparin and dabigatran and to major fibrinogen problems.

- **Fibrinogen (Clauss)** is central to obstetric and traumatic bleeding; a falling fibrinogen may precede other conventional abnormalities.
- **D-dimer** indicates cross-linked fibrin turnover but is nonspecific after surgery, infection, pregnancy or trauma.
- **Blood film** can reveal schistocytes (microangiopathy), blasts, abnormal cells, platelet clumping or haemolysis.
- **Mixing studies** help distinguish a factor deficiency (correction) from an inhibitor (no correction or time-dependent loss of correction), but interpretation needs laboratory support.

- **Viscoelastic methods (ROTEM/TEG)** assess evolving whole-blood clot formation and strength under low shear: initiation, fibrin/polymerisation, platelet contribution and lysis.
- They are valuable during active bleeding because they can direct specific component replacement faster than waiting for serial conventional results, but they are not perfect measures of in-vivo endothelial haemostasis and have limited sensitivity to aspirin, some DOACs, vWF disease and some platelet defects.
- The local assay and cartridge determine what a result means; do not interchange ROTEM and TEG numerical thresholds.

| **Test or pattern** | **Interpretation** | **Appropriate response in a bleeding patient** |
|---|---|---|
| Long CT/R-time, low clot initiation | Factor deficiency, anticoagulant effect, sometimes residual heparin | Identify drug; plasma or specific reversal when indicated |
| Reduced fibrin contribution (e.g. FIBTEM A5/A10) | Fibrinogen deficit/poor polymerisation | Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate using validated local algorithm |
| Reduced whole clot strength with adequate fibrin | Platelet count/function deficit | Platelets if indicated; investigate cause |
| Rapid clot lysis | Hyperfibrinolysis | Consider TXA when appropriate to scenario/timing |
| All tests apparently satisfactory but bleeding continues | Surgical source or defect not captured by test | Reassess surgical source, temperature, calcium, drugs and clinical context |

## 1.3 Core physiology in haemorrhage

- Oxygen delivery is approximately **DO₂ = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content**; arterial oxygen content is predominantly haemoglobin-bound O₂ (approximately 1.34 × Hb[g/dL] × saturation).
- Acute blood loss therefore impairs oxygen delivery through both falling circulating volume and, after redistribution/resuscitation, lower Hb.
- Initially, measured haemoglobin may be misleadingly normal because red cells and plasma are lost together.
- A low Hb later does not establish that ongoing hypoperfusion is solely an oxygen-carrying problem: search for inadequate cardiac output, hypoxia, low perfusion pressure and continued haemorrhage.

- Haemorrhage also impairs haemostasis via hypoperfusion, endothelial injury, consumption, and resuscitation-associated dilution.
- **Hypothermia** suppresses platelet and enzyme function; **acidosis** reduces thrombin generation and myocardial performance; **hypocalcaemia** reduces coagulation and contractility.
- These effects may reinforce one another, but there is no single fixed “lethal triad” threshold at which bleeding becomes irreversible.
- The definitive intervention remains control of the source.

### A bleeding patient with isolated abnormal coagulation tests

A useful diagnostic mini-algorithm:

| **Finding** | **Prioritised differential** | **Next clinical decision** |
|---|---|---|
| Isolated prolonged PT | Warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, early liver synthetic impairment, factor VII deficit | Check drug/nutrition; determine bleeding need for reversal |
| Isolated prolonged APTT | UFH, factor VIII/IX/XI deficiencies, acquired FVIII inhibitor, lupus anticoagulant, contact factor deficits | Heparin exposure/thrombin time; mixing study and targeted factor/inhibitor assays |
| Both PT and APTT prolonged | DIC, massive dilution, advanced liver disease, common pathway deficit, high DOAC concentration | Assess clinical phenotype, fibrinogen, platelets, drug history |
| Platelet count normal but oozing | Antiplatelet drug, uraemia, vWD, acquired platelet dysfunction, hypothermia | Treat cause; consider functional testing or targeted treatment |
| Low fibrinogen with high D-dimer | Severe consumption/hyperfibrinolysis, liver disease, dilution | Replace fibrinogen in active bleeding; treat driver |
| Markedly prolonged APTT but thrombosis | Lupus anticoagulant or other inhibitor, anticoagulant exposure | Do not assume bleeding risk from APTT alone |

- A mixing study is a **clue** rather than a final diagnosis: a deficiency generally corrects, whereas an inhibitor often does not, but some inhibitors (e.g. acquired FVIII inhibitor) are time-dependent.
- Lupus anticoagulant can prolong phospholipid-dependent assays while increasing thrombosis risk.
- An isolated prolonged APTT from factor XII deficiency typically does not cause clinical bleeding.
- These distinctions are a common opportunity to demonstrate physiologic understanding in a viva.

items.title: 2. Preoperative assessment: anaemia, bleeding risk and thrombosis
items.body:
## 2.1 Why preoperative anaemia matters

- Anaemia is associated with increased transfusion, complications, length of stay and mortality; it should be treated as a **diagnosis to investigate**, not a number to accept or a reason to give prophylactic RBCs.
- For patients undergoing major surgery, many PBM pathways use Hb <130 g/L in either sex to trigger evaluation, because expected blood loss is not sex-adjusted.
- This is a practical perioperative screening threshold rather than the definition of every population’s anaemia.

**History:**

- Bleeding (GI, menstrual, urinary), nutrition/diet, malabsorption, CKD, inflammation, haemoglobinopathy, haemolysis, previous transfusion/reactions, symptoms of reduced reserve, anti-thrombotics and prior anaemia treatment.
- **Tests:** CBC and indices, reticulocyte count, ferritin and transferrin saturation (TSAT), CRP when inflammation suspected, renal function, B12/folate selectively, blood film if unexplained.
- Iron deficiency typically shows ferritin <30 μg/L; in inflammation ferritin can be falsely normal/high, so TSAT <20% with ferritin <100 μg/L can support deficiency depending on context.
- Ferritin <100 μg/L may also be regarded as inadequate stores for major surgery where erythropoietic demands are high.
- Investigate the cause of iron loss, including malignancy when relevant.

| **Anaemia** | **Clues** | **Management before major elective surgery** |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute iron deficiency | Low MCV (not always), low ferritin, low TSAT, high TIBC | Treat source; oral iron if time/tolerated, IV iron for short interval, intolerance, functional deficiency or greater deficit |
| Inflammation / functional iron deficiency | Ferritin normal/high with TSAT low, CRP high | Treat underlying inflammation; IV iron only after considering indication/infection risk |
| CKD | Often normocytic, low reticulocyte response | Check iron; consider ESA in selected CKD patients with specialist input; manage thrombosis risk |
| B12 / folate deficiency | Macrocytosis, cytopenias ± neurological symptoms (B12) | Replace specific deficiency; avoid treating B12 deficit with folate alone |
| Haemolysis | Raised reticulocytes, bilirubin/LDH; low haptoglobin | Identify immune, mechanical or hereditary cause |
| Marrow disease | Reticulocytopenia ± other cytopenias / abnormal film | Haematology assessment, definitive diagnosis |

**Timing and optimisation:**

- Identify anaemia weeks before surgery; oral iron may require several weeks and is limited by adverse effects/absorption.
- IV iron improves Hb more quickly and avoids enteral intolerance, but does not reliably reduce transfusion or complications in every surgical population (PREVENTT trial).
- Do not interpret negative trial outcomes as a reason never to correct iron deficiency; correct genuine deficiency while managing expectations and the underlying disease.
- ESAs are selective rather than routine because of thrombotic risks.
- For time-sensitive surgery, discuss expected blood loss, availability of cell salvage, blood products, postoperative monitoring and the consequences of proceeding before full correction.

### Putting anaemia assessment into a real preadmission timeline

- If a patient is listed for major elective surgery in **six weeks**, screen now rather than the day before surgery.
- A full blood count and ferritin/TSAT identify iron deficiency and whether an inflammatory component is likely.
- For a patient with ferritin 15 μg/L, Hb 106 g/L and significant expected operative blood loss, address menstrual/GI blood loss, offer iron replacement and reassess Hb after an interval adequate to demonstrate response.
- Failure of Hb to rise despite treatment should prompt investigation of ongoing blood loss, nonadherence, inflammation, concurrent B12/folate deficiency or alternative diagnosis.
- In a patient with ferritin 250 μg/L and TSAT 12%, do not prescribe high-dose iron automatically: evaluate inflammation, CKD and infection, and decide whether functional deficiency is clinically relevant.
- The point is **optimisation of the oxygen-carrying system and treatment of underlying disease**, not temporary correction of a result by transfusion.

- If surgery cannot be deferred, estimate the expected blood loss, reserve blood where indicated, use appropriate TXA and cell salvage, and document what degree of anaemia is acceptable given the patient’s cardiopulmonary reserve.
- For a patient with recent MI, angina, significant aortic stenosis or symptomatic HF, the risk of low oxygen content differs from a healthy patient undergoing a short low-bleeding-risk operation.
- The eventual intraoperative transfusion threshold must be tied to physiology and active bleeding.
- The timing and logistics of IV iron do not justify postponing cancer surgery automatically; multidisciplinary discussion is required.

## 2.2 A focused bleeding history is more useful than routine coagulation tests in everyone

- Ask about previous operations, dental extraction, postpartum bleeding, epistaxis, heavy menstrual bleeding, easy bruising, spontaneous deep haemorrhage, family history, liver or renal disease and prescribed/OTC agents (aspirin, antiplatelets, DOACs, warfarin, NSAIDs and supplements).
- A structured bleeding-assessment tool may help in selected cases.
- Routine preoperative PT/APTT in low-risk asymptomatic patients has limited predictive value; investigate when history, disease, procedure or medication suggests risk.
- For known severe bleeding disorder, plan factor therapy, neuraxial safety, blood product availability and an agreed haematology protocol in advance.

### An inherited bleeding disorder presents for major surgery

- A previously diagnosed **haemophilia A** patient needs total knee replacement.
- The mechanism is deficiency of factor VIII, typically X-linked, causing impaired intrinsic tenase activity and therefore reduced thrombin amplification.
- Severe deficiency (<1% factor activity) produces spontaneous haemarthrosis, muscular bleeding and joint damage; moderate disease (1–5%) may cause trauma-related haemorrhage, and mild disease (>5–40%) may first present with surgical bleeding.
- APTT may be prolonged but can be normal in mild disease; factor VIII assay and inhibitor screen are more useful.
- Factor VIII is carried by vWF in circulation.
- Repeated factor exposure can induce an inhibitor that makes standard replacement ineffective, and older blood products created important viral infection history.

**Preoperative plan:**

- Define baseline factor activity, previous replacement/inhibitor titre, bleeding phenotype, arthropathy/airway issues, liver disease, HIV/hepatitis history, target factor activity for the procedure, availability of recombinant factor concentrate and a daily postoperative factor plan agreed with haematology.
- For major surgery aim for high perioperative factor VIII activity (often around 80–100% initially), with an agreed taper over days as healing proceeds; dosing and trough targets are individualised.
- Recombinant FVIII is standard for non-inhibitor haemophilia A; desmopressin may suit selected mild patients with a proven adequate response, but is inadequate for most major surgery in severe disease.
- Emicizumab prophylaxis changes bleeding risk and confounds APTT-based FVIII assays; additional perioperative factor or bypassing agents may still be required.
- In inhibitors, specialist agents such as recombinant VIIa or activated PCC can be indicated; combinations have thrombosis/TMA risks in emicizumab-treated patients.

**Intraoperative plan:**

- Reliable factor coverage before incision, atraumatic airway/vascular techniques, monitored blood loss, TXA as an adjunct where appropriate, meticulous haemostasis and avoidance of NSAIDs that worsen platelet function.
- Neuraxial analgesia is not automatically allowed merely because a single dose of factor was given; assess factor activity throughout catheter presence and removal, inhibitor status, procedure risk and specialist agreement.
- **Postoperative:** continue factor support through wound healing/physiotherapy, monitor bleeds into joint or muscle, check factor levels/inhibitors, and balance VTE prophylaxis against the patient’s restored clotting capacity and major orthopaedic risk.

- **Haemophilia B** is factor IX deficiency and requires FIX replacement, not FVIII.

**Von Willebrand disease** impairs platelet adhesion and sometimes FVIII carriage:

- Type 1 quantitative partial deficiency.
- Type 2 qualitative dysfunction.
- Type 3 profound absence.

- Typical bleeding is mucocutaneous, menorrhagia or surgical ooze, rather than only spontaneous haemarthrosis.
- Tests include vWF antigen, activity, FVIII and specialised multimers as needed.
- Desmopressin is useful in selected type 1 patients after a documented trial; type 2B may develop thrombocytopenia with desmopressin, and type 3 generally needs vWF concentrate.
- Give TXA for mucosal bleeding where appropriate; monitor sodium after desmopressin because water retention can cause hyponatraemia.

### Turn the haemophilia history into a safe operative factor plan

- A practical calculation matters: an intravenous dose of 1 IU/kg of factor VIII typically raises plasma FVIII activity by about 2 IU/dL (2 percentage points) in an adult, although recovery varies.
- If baseline activity is 2% and the target is 100%, the approximate loading dose is (100 − 2) × weight (kg) ÷ 2 IU; verify product pharmacokinetics, baseline recovery, any inhibitor, and the actual measured level.
- FIX dosing is product-specific and cannot use the FVIII formula.
- The key safety requirement is documenting a target level, timing before incision, serial trough measurements, postoperative duration and a funded/available product supply—not simply prescribing one preoperative bolus.

| **Condition** | **Typical screening pattern** | **Perioperative treatment logic** |
|---|---|---|
| Haemophilia A (FVIII) | Deep tissue/haemarthrosis; normal PT, often prolonged APTT (can be normal in mild disease); low FVIII assay | Major surgery: specialist plan often targets FVIII 80–100 IU/dL before incision, then taper with measured levels over 7–14 days depending on procedure and bleeding. Recombinant FVIII; emicizumab/inhibitor status alters testing and rescue. |
| Haemophilia B (FIX) | Similar phenotype; FIX deficiency, normal PT and often prolonged APTT | FIX concentrate with product- and patient-specific pharmacokinetics; major-surgery target generally somewhat lower than FVIII protocols; monitor FIX activity and inhibitor. |
| von Willebrand disease | Mucocutaneous bleeding, postpartum or surgical oozing; PT normal; APTT often normal, may increase if FVIII low | Obtain VWF antigen/activity and FVIII; DDAVP only if type/response appropriate; VWF concentrate and TXA as indicated. Major surgery: guide therapy by both FVIII and VWF activity, not FVIII alone. |
| Acquired FVIII inhibitor | New severe soft-tissue bleeding, no family history; isolated prolonged APTT, time-dependent mixing-test failure | Urgent haematology; bypassing haemostatic therapy or recombinant porcine FVIII in selected cases plus inhibitor eradication. Do not assume ordinary FVIII concentrate will work. |

- For haemophilia A undergoing major surgery, the commonly taught WFH ranges are FVIII 80–100 IU/dL preoperatively, approximately 60–80 during postoperative days 1–3, 40–60 on days 4–6, and 30–50 on days 7–14.
- These are specialist targets, not a prescription to transfuse everyone to one level; an individualised regimen depends on procedure, factor product, inhibitor status and measured recovery.
- Factor support must extend through wound healing and rehabilitation, not stop when the epidural/spinal needle is withdrawn.

- For von Willebrand disease, the ASH/ISTH/NHF/WFH 2021 guideline suggests keeping both FVIII and VWF activity at or above 0.50 IU/mL for at least 3 days after major surgery, extended as clinically indicated.
- A DDAVP trial helps in responsive type 1 disease; avoid assuming effectiveness in type 3 disease or safety in type 2B, and monitor sodium/fluid restriction.
- TXA is helpful for mucosal sites but not a substitute for systemic factor replacement during major surgery.
- Discuss perioperative thromboprophylaxis separately after factor correction because restoring clotting activity can restore clinically important VTE risk.

## 2.3 Anticoagulants and antiplatelets: balance two different hazards

- Stopping treatment increases thrombosis risk, whereas continuing increases surgical/neuraxial bleeding risk.
- Define **indication, date of index event, renal function, dose, last administration, planned procedure and bleeding risk**.
- Distinguish prophylactic versus therapeutic anticoagulation and distinguish surgery timing from regional anaesthesia timing.
- A routine elective management table cannot replace current ASRA/ANZCA/local neuraxial rules.

| **Class** | **Mechanism / relevant assay** | **Planning principle** |
|---|---|---|
| Warfarin | Vitamin K-dependent II, VII, IX, X; INR | Usually interrupt ≈5 days before high-bleeding-risk surgery and verify INR; bridge only selected very high thrombosis-risk patients |
| Dabigatran | Direct IIa; dilute thrombin time/ecarin if available | Hold according to bleeding risk and renal function; idarucizumab for urgent reversal where indicated |
| Apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban | Direct Xa; calibrated drug-specific anti-Xa | Hold according to procedure, kidney function and dosing; avoid using normal INR/APTT to exclude activity |
| UFH | Antithrombin-mediated IIa/Xa; APTT or anti-Xa | Short half-life; protamine reverses, dose accounts for recent heparin exposure |
| LMWH | Predominantly Xa; anti-Xa when needed | Longer effect with renal impairment; protamine only partly reverses anti-Xa effect |
| Aspirin | Irreversible COX-1 | Consider reason (PCI/secondary prevention), surgical bleeding and neuraxial context |
| Clopidogrel/ticagrelor/prasugrel | P2Y₁₂ inhibition | PCI timing and stent thrombosis risk crucial; neuraxial and surgical interruption windows differ |

**When to delay:**

- An active unstable VTE, recent high-risk thrombosis, severe uncorrected coagulopathy or marked cytopenia may justify postponement of elective surgery.
- Recent VTE (especially within three months), high-risk mechanical valves and recent coronary stents require specialist planning, but all are different thrombotic syndromes.
- Document the agreed postoperative restart date and any bridging/indwelling catheter restrictions before theatre.

items.title: 3. Patient blood management: prevent blood loss before transfusing
items.body:
## 3.1 The three PBM pillars

- Patient blood management is a systematic approach to improve outcomes by **optimising the patient’s own red-cell mass, minimising blood loss, and improving tolerance of anaemia**.
- All three should start before incision and continue through postoperative care.
- This is more useful for an ANZCA ‘critically evaluate’ LO than simply reciting a shopping list: each intervention must be matched to the source of blood loss, evidence, harms and logistics.

**Preoperative pillar:**

- Identify and treat anaemia, review anticoagulants/antiplatelets and bleeding disorders, plan crossmatch/special blood requirements, assess procedural bleeding risk, obtain consent for transfusion alternatives and discuss anticipated ICU care.
- Pregnancy/alloantibodies, rare blood type, multiple transfusions or refusal of some products require early blood-bank involvement.

**Intraoperative pillar:**

- Precise surgical haemostasis, minimally invasive/interventional techniques when suitable, TXA in the right indication, cell salvage when appropriate, maintaining normothermia/pH/iCa, rational fluids, restrictive diagnostic blood sampling and goal-directed replacement when clinically necessary.
- Deliberate hypotension is **not universally safe** in patients with CAD, cerebrovascular disease, reduced organ reserve or ongoing major bleeding.
- Regional techniques can decrease bleeding for some operations but must be balanced against systemic effects and antithrombotic safety.

**Postoperative pillar:**

- Actively search for ongoing bleeding, maintain temperature, reduce phlebotomy and repeated unnecessary labs, prevent/treat infection, continue iron replacement where indicated, give single-unit RBCs with reassessment for the stable nonbleeding patient, and treat low Hb with clinical context rather than an arbitrary target.
- Avoid unnecessary transfusion because it brings risks including reactions, TACO, alloimmunisation and infection (now rare with screened components).

## 3.2 Tranexamic acid — mechanism, indications and limitations

- TXA is a synthetic lysine analogue that blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin; it inhibits clot breakdown but does not replace coagulation factors or treat an unsecured bleeding vessel.
- Benefits are procedure- and timing-dependent.
- It is useful in major trauma when started **within 3 hours of injury** and in postpartum haemorrhage within 3 hours of birth; late use in trauma may be harmful (CRASH-2 subgroup) and should not be copied indiscriminately to all bleeding situations.
- In elective major orthopaedic and other selected surgery, it reduces blood loss/transfusion.
- In cardiac surgery, larger doses may increase seizures; choose a validated regimen and adjust for renal clearance.

**Example regimens (verify local protocol):**

- Major trauma often 1 g IV over 10 min followed by 1 g over 8 h; PPH 1 g IV over 10 min, repeat 1 g if bleeding persists after 30 min or recurs within 24 h; elective surgical dosing varies widely and is not interchangeable across specialties.
- TXA is not a substitute for immediate surgery, embolisation, balanced resuscitation or appropriate thromboprophylaxis.

- **Evidence:** CRASH-2 (trauma), WOMAN (PPH), POISE-3 (major noncardiac surgery) and ATACAS (cardiac surgery) inform different indications; their populations and benefits must not be conflated.

## 3.3 Intraoperative cell salvage — understand the actual circuit

- The **Carroll and Young BJA Education 2021** article is the primary learning reference.
- Cell salvage is most valuable when significant shed blood is expected (commonly consider if blood loss may exceed **500 mL**, or >10% estimated blood volume), particularly major vascular, revision orthopaedic, trauma, cardiac and selected obstetric procedures.
- It avoids donor exposure and provides an autologous oxygen-carrying product, especially useful when crossmatching is difficult.

**The process: COLLECTION → RESERVOIR/FILTRATION → CENTRIFUGATION → WASHING → REINFUSION.**

![Intraoperative cell salvage circuit](set2-fig1.png)

| **Benefit** | **Limitation or risk** |
|---|---|
| Less donor RBC exposure; immediately available autologous cells | Training, staff, dedicated circuit and operating cost |
| Preserves RBC oxygen-carrying capacity | No fibrinogen/platelet replacement; no intrinsic correction of coagulopathy |
| Particularly valuable with antibodies or some blood-refusal preferences | Individual informed consent; some patients accept only continuous closed circuits |
| Useful in high-blood-loss surgery | Haemolysis from excessive suction, air embolus risk, dilution, hypotension during reinfusion; meticulous identification needed |
| Possible use in sepsis/malignancy with mitigation | Not automatically contraindicated, but contamination requires risk assessment, clean suction, washing and appropriate filtration |

**Contamination/safety:**

- Divert suction during topical haemostatics, iodine/chlorhexidine, non-IV antibiotics, unset bone cement, urine or faecal contamination.
- Lipid or leucocyte-depletion filters may mitigate specific risks but restrict flow; their ability to remove every contaminant is not absolute.
- With malignancy, leucocyte depletion may reduce tumour-cell return; local policy and surgical/haematology discussion are needed.
- In sepsis and contaminated fields, there is no blanket absolute prohibition, but avoid collecting gross pus/heavily contaminated material.
- Sickle cell disease/trait or fragile cells warrant specialist advice because centrifugation/oxygenation may damage or sickle erythrocytes.
- For obstetrics discuss amniotic contamination, leucocyte filtration and local protocols.
- **If the patient refuses donor products, document exactly which elements of salvage they accept rather than assuming consent.**

### Critical evaluation

- Cell salvage reduces exposure to allogeneic transfusion in suitable surgeries, but it is not cost-effective when expected blood loss is trivial
- Volume of salvage may be insufficient in fast exsanguination
- Trained staff and contamination avoidance are essential
- And the RBC-only product does not correct a dilutional coagulopathy.
- The 2024.2 ANZCA SAQ required the functional elements of collection, processing and administration as well as indications/advantages/disadvantages.
- Explaining the physical circuit is more examinable than merely saying ‘use cell saver’.

### Cell-salvage decisions during different operations

**Major revision hip surgery:**

- Anticipated 1–2 L blood loss makes salvage attractive, especially if preoperative anaemia or complex antibodies are present.
- Use a separate salvage suction circuit and avoid collecting unset bone cement, topical haemostatic agents or major nonblood contaminants.
- Some systems permit swab washing; the fluid must be appropriate for intravenous use, and labelling/traceability are vital.
- The resulting RBC product is useful for oxygen carriage but does not replace surgical haemostasis or clotting factors.

**Oncological laparotomy:**

- Historically salvage was avoided because of possible tumour-cell reinfusion.
- Modern literature and leukocyte depletion have expanded selected use, but assessment depends on tumour type, contamination and local policy.
- Do not claim absolute zero risk or that all cancer cases are contraindicated.
- **Contaminated bowel surgery:** separate grossly faecal-contaminated suction and weigh infection risk versus life-threatening blood loss.
- **Obstetrics:** assess risk of amniotic-fluid contamination, use established maternity-specific protocols and discuss available filtration; this is especially relevant to placenta accreta surgery.
- **Jehovah’s Witnesses:** the patient’s acceptance of a continuous circuit, anticoagulant and washed autologous blood is individual; document each choice.

- There are also timing and human-factor limitations: a centrifuge may not have accumulated enough cells for its first cycle when a patient is abruptly exsanguinating; emergency donor RBCs may still be required if acceptable.
- A slow cell-salvage process can distract from source control if roles are unclear.
- Have separate trained personnel, quality checks, an escalation plan and rapid communication about the volume actually available for reinfusion.

## 3.4 Other blood conservation techniques

**Acute normovolaemic haemodilution:**

- Before major blood loss, remove autologous whole blood while maintaining intravascular volume with appropriate replacement; return it later so the collected blood retains platelets/coagulation factors.
- Lower operative Hb means fewer red cells lost per litre of bleeding, but benefits depend on case selection, baseline Hb, anticipated loss, workflow and cardiovascular tolerance; not standard for all patients.

**Autologous predeposit:**

- May reduce donor use but can induce preoperative anaemia, waste blood and is less useful under modern PBM; reserve for unusual circumstances.
- **Controlled hypotension:** can reduce bleeding in selected surgery, but reduces perfusion in vulnerable patients.
- **Haemostatic surgical techniques** include early vascular control, topical haemostats, embolisation, tourniquets, meticulous tissue handling and damage-control surgery; these often matter more than pharmacological adjuncts.
- **Laboratory conservation** in ICU includes paediatric tubes and reducing unnecessary sampling.

### How to choose the remaining blood-conservation options

- These techniques are not interchangeable.

The useful sequence is:

- (1) correct preoperative anaemia and the cause of bleeding.
- (2) minimise actual surgical bleeding.
- (3) consider autologous recovery or pharmacological adjuncts when the expected loss justifies them.
- (4) preserve oxygen delivery and organ perfusion throughout.

- A reduction in measured blood loss is not, by itself, proof of fewer important complications.

| **Strategy** | **Mechanism and ideal situation** | **Limitations / important contraindications** |
|---|---|---|
| Acute normovolaemic haemodilution (ANH) | Shortly after induction, collect autologous whole blood with appropriate labelling and storage while maintaining normovolaemia. A lower circulating red-cell concentration means fewer RBCs lost with each subsequent litre of bleeding; reinfuse later to return RBCs, platelets and functional clotting factors. Most plausible in selected patients with normal/high baseline Hb and large predictable surgical loss. | Avoid a fall in oxygen delivery in patients with marked anaemia, major active ischaemia, severe fixed-output cardiac disease or limited physiological reserve. Extra staff, accurate volume replacement and reinfusion protocol required. Evidence is variable and procedure dependent. |
| Deliberate controlled hypotension | In selected low-risk, elective procedures it may reduce arterial/venous oozing and improve the field when combined with appropriate position, surgical haemostasis and anaesthetic control. | Avoid in hypovolaemia/active haemorrhagic shock or when cerebral, coronary, renal or spinal perfusion is threatened. No universal “20% below baseline” target is proven safe; avoid prolonged MAP <60–65 mmHg and individualise higher targets. |
| Preoperative autologous donation | Predeposit patient’s own RBC units in advance for a narrowly defined expected need (e.g. rare antibody profile with adequate Hb and time). | Can cause preoperative anaemia, leads to unused-unit waste and introduces collection/storage/transfusion errors; usually inferior to modern anaemia optimisation and cell salvage. |
| Surgical/anaesthetic techniques | Meticulous haemostasis, minimally invasive access where appropriate, tourniquet, haemostatic agents, embolisation, regional technique where safe, normothermia and avoidance of unnecessary dilution. | Each depends on operation; tourniquets and topical agents carry site-specific thrombotic, tissue and contamination risks; regional anaesthesia is constrained by anticoagulation and hypotension. |

- Evidence nuance: the large 2025 multinational ANH RCT in CPB cardiac surgery (n≈2,010) found allogeneic RBC transfusion in 27.3% versus 29.2% (RR 0.93; P=0.34), so it did not demonstrate that routine ANH reduced transfusion incidence.
- A later meta-analysis pooling heterogeneous smaller studies suggested an average reduction, but heterogeneity and procedure differences are important; avoid presenting ANH as definitively beneficial or useless in every operation.
- This is a particularly good example of what “critically evaluate” means in an ANZCA answer.

- Deliberate hypotension should be a consciously chosen anaesthetic intervention, not a euphemism for untreated hypotension.
- Before considering it, establish vascular/cerebrovascular disease, coronary reserve, haemoglobin, expected duration, positioning (e.g. head-up beach chair), level of arterial measurement relative to the brain, and an agreed end point with the surgeon.
- Continuous BP monitoring may be appropriate; stop the strategy if there is evidence of organ ischaemia or insufficient perfusion.
- In higher-risk patients, a dry surgical field is not worth myocardial injury, AKI or stroke.

items.title: 4. Major haemorrhage and trauma/surgery-associated coagulopathy
items.priority: P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 4.1 Recognise a major haemorrhage before the haemoglobin falls

- Major bleeding is a clinical emergency, not a threshold reached only after a stated number of RBC units.
- Look for rapid overt loss, falling arterial pressure/pulse pressure, increasing heart rate (may be absent under beta-blockade/anaesthesia), altered perfusion/mental status, rising lactate/base deficit, low urine output, vasopressor need and escalating transfusion requirement.
- In theatre, ongoing suction loss is often underestimated because blood soaks into swabs or hides in body cavities.
- Early Hb can remain normal; serial Hb alongside haemodynamics, coagulation and operative observations are needed.

**First priorities:**

- Call for help and activate the institution’s major haemorrhage protocol (MHP), stop the bleeding through surgery/packing/embolisation, protect the airway and oxygenation, secure large-bore access and warming devices, send type/crossmatch and baseline studies (CBC, PT/APTT, fibrinogen, ionised Ca, gas, lactate ± VEM).
- Communicate an estimate of the time to achieve haemostasis to blood bank, surgery, ICU, radiology and theatre staff.
- Avoid large unstructured crystalloid loads because they dilute factors, impair temperature and cannot replace oxygen-carrying capacity.

![Major haemorrhage loop](set2-fig2.png)

Major haemorrhage loop

## 4.2 Why early balanced components are used

- Before full results return, massive bleeding with plasma and platelet losses needs an empiric **ratio-based MHP**, not RBCs alone.
- Once conventional and VEM results become available, shift to **goal-directed therapy**.
- The 2023 Australian NBA adult critical bleeding guideline (minor update September 2025) suggests at least **1 unit FFP per 2 RBC units** and at least **one adult platelet unit per 8 RBC units** during ratio-based support.
- This is a minimum ratio recommendation, not a universal 1:1:1 mandate or an instruction to wait until eight units have been given before platelets.
- Many local protocols target higher early ratios, especially in trauma.
- Use institutional pack design and integrate monitoring rather than inventing a single correct pack.

- The **PROPPR** trauma trial compared 1:1:1 with 1:1:2 plasma:platelets:RBC strategies: overall 24-hour and 30-day mortality differences were not statistically significant, but early haemostasis and deaths from exsanguination favoured the 1:1:1 strategy.
- This informs early component delivery; it does not establish that high ratios are optimal indefinitely or for every non-traumatic bleeding cause.

### Suggested bedside targets during active major bleeding

| **Variable** | **Why it matters** | **Common goal or response** |
|---|---|---|
| Platelets | Primary haemostasis | Commonly aim >50 ×10⁹/L during major bleeding, higher (≈100) with intracranial/critical-site bleeding; integrate function |
| Fibrinogen | Clot firmness and stability | Replace if <1.5–2.0 g/L in critical bleeding; obstetrics often warrants at least ≈2.0 g/L; use local VEM triggers |
| INR/APTT | Factor deficiency/anticoagulants | Correct major clinically relevant abnormalities in bleeding, not isolated mildly raised tests without bleeding |
| Ionised calcium | Needed for coagulation and contractility | Monitor repeatedly and maintain physiologic iCa (often around ≥1.1–1.2 mmol/L by local protocol) |
| Temperature | Enzyme and platelet function | Warm actively, target normothermia |
| pH / lactate | Perfusion, enzymatic activity | Restore perfusion/source control rather than simply ‘correcting’ laboratory acidosis |
| Hb | Oxygen carriage | In active exsanguination, interpret with rate of loss and perfusion; stable 70 g/L thresholds do not apply rigidly |

**Fibrinogen replacement:**

- The NBA offers a guide of **3–4 g fibrinogen**, given as fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate (in NZ a pragmatic guide is around **1 unit of cryoprecipitate per 30 kg** depending on product/pool; confirm local dose).
- Recheck the measured fibrinogen/VEM and clinical bleeding.
- Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, vWF, VIII and XIII; concentrate provides a standardised fibrinogen dose with small volume.
- **Platelets:** one adult therapeutic dose (apheresis or pooled equivalent) generally increases count by ≈20–40 ×10⁹/L in a nonconsuming adult, less with ongoing haemorrhage, DIC, splenomegaly or sepsis.
- **FFP:** replaces multiple soluble factors but requires substantial volume, is slow to thaw and is inefficient for correcting an isolated mild INR increase.
- **PCC:** rapid vitamin K-dependent factor replacement for indicated warfarin reversal; not equivalent to FFP for all acquired coagulopathies and carries thrombotic risk.

### Point-of-care haemostasis: how to interpret and critically evaluate it

- The 2025.2 ANZCA SAQ explicitly asked candidates to **evaluate point-of-care testing modalities during acute intraoperative haemorrhage**.
- The ANZCA 2025 Blue Book chapter by Hegde and colleagues on goal-directed bleeding management places rapid viscoelastic assays within a wider patient blood-management approach rather than using a one-size-fits-all transfusion ratio indefinitely.
- A high-quality answer should first distinguish rapid decision support from the idea that every instrument directly measures what is happening within a surgical wound.

**Blood gas analyser:**

- Rapid Hb (depending on modality), pH, lactate, ionised Ca and electrolytes.
- It detects physiological consequences and correctable metabolic derangements but does **not** diagnose fibrinogen/platelet/factor deficits.
- Point-of-care Hb varies with dilution/sample method and needs trend/laboratory corroboration.
- **ACT:** useful for high-dose heparin in CPB/interventions but is affected by hypothermia, haemodilution, platelet disorders and contact activation; not a generic MHP test and not reliable to quantify DOAC effect.
- **INR point-of-care:** convenient for warfarin monitoring, but may be unreliable with lupus anticoagulant, extreme values, some DOACs and critical illness.
- **Platelet-function tests** (e.g. aggregometry, PFA, VerifyNow) may quantify selected antiplatelet effects but have context-dependent correlations with surgical bleeding and cannot replace clinical haemostasis or direct drug history.

**VEM details:**

- TEG/ROTEM combine initiation (R or CT), clot kinetics (K/CFT and alpha angle), peak strength (MA/MCF), fibrin contribution (functional fibrinogen/FIBTEM) and fibrinolysis.
- They differ by activators, reagents and normal ranges.
- If a fibrin-specific trace is weak, replace fibrinogen
- If overall trace is weak after fibrin correction, consider platelets
- If initiation is prolonged, investigate factors, anticoagulants and calcium
- If excessive lysis, consider TXA in the appropriate time window.
- **Limitations:** measurements are ex-vivo at specific conditions
- Platelet inhibition by aspirin/P2Y₁₂ may be missed
- Tests poorly detect vWF dysfunction
- No endothelium, dynamic vascular injury or local tissue-factor gradients
- Sampling and processing artefacts
- Cost/training
- Results can appear ‘normal’ despite active surgical bleeding.
- Transfusion algorithms may reduce product exposure but not every study demonstrates a mortality benefit.

- **How to answer the 2025.2 question:** for each modality say what it measures → return time → which treatment it guides → limitations → where it fits within haemorrhage control. A mere list ‘TEG, ROTEM, ACT, Hb’ is not an evaluation.

### Where factor-guided haemostasis changes the management

- Suppose after controlling an aortic bleeding point, a patient continues to ooze diffusely and the initial MHP pack has delivered several RBC and plasma units.
- The platelet count is 82 ×10⁹/L, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, INR 1.4 and ionised calcium 0.87 mmol/L.
- More RBC alone will improve oxygen content but will not establish a durable clot.
- **Correct marked hypofibrinogenaemia and hypocalcaemia**, continue active warming and reassess the surgical field while monitoring response.
- If platelet count/functional clot strength then falls, address the platelet component.
- Small FFP doses solely to reduce INR 1.4 to 1.2 may be ineffective and add volume.
- If the field remains briskly bleeding from an artery, a perfect VEM trace cannot compensate for source control.

- Now consider the opposite: fibrinogen 3.1 g/L, platelets 170 ×10⁹/L and near-normal VEM clot formation, yet suction loss remains 500 mL every five minutes.
- Escalate surgical haemostasis and imaging/embolisation instead of reflexively transfusing fibrinogen, platelets and plasma.
- This is the clinical value of the VEM concept: **give what the clot lacks**, but remember the clot is not the only reason a patient bleeds.

**VEM-guided algorithms are not universal recipes:**

- Some products can shorten initiation time yet raise thrombotic risk, particularly high-dose PCC given empirically to a patient without vitamin K-factor deficiency.
- Verify the exact reagent/cartridge (e.g. EXTEM, INTEM, FIBTEM, HEPTEM in ROTEM), instrument ranges and local major-bleeding pathway.
- An isolated prolonged CT may represent heparin effect rather than a factor deficiency; comparison of heparinase and non-heparinase channels can avoid unnecessary plasma.
- At the same time, an apparently reassuring standard ROTEM may not reveal a patient taking clopidogrel or with vWF dysfunction.

### Worked point-of-care patterns: what product is actually missing?

- Read the patient before reading the trace: surgical source control, temperature, ionised calcium, pH, shock and anticoagulant exposure remain essential.
- Viscoelastic testing measures clot initiation, firmness and lysis in whole blood; it does not measure endothelial contribution, vessel injury, all platelet defects or every anticoagulant.
- Interpret the ROTEM channels as complementary questions—not isolated abnormal numbers.

| **Pattern in a patient actively bleeding** | **Interpretation** | **Next action and limitation** |
|---|---|---|
| EXTEM CT prolonged; FIBTEM firmness near normal | Delayed clot initiation suggests deficiency/inhibition of coagulation factors. Compare PT/APTT and heparin effect; exclude sample, anticoagulant or severe physiological problems. | Consider plasma/factor-directed treatment per local major-bleeding protocol if clinically indicated. Do not assume every long CT requires PCC, particularly in trauma with thrombosis risk. |
| FIBTEM A5 very low (e.g. <10 mm in a protocol using that cut-off), with weak EXTEM | Low fibrin-based clot contribution, often due to fibrinogen depletion/dysfunction. | Give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate according to protocol; repeat fibrinogen/viscoelastic test. Use your laboratory’s validated A5 threshold. |
| Weak EXTEM clot but preserved FIBTEM | Fibrin contribution relatively adequate; low platelet number or function is more likely. | Check platelet count and exposure to antiplatelet agents/CPB; consider platelet transfusion in clinically important bleeding. VEM cannot replace platelet-function tests. |
| INTEM CT prolonged, corrects with HEPTEM | Supports an effect from unfractionated heparin or heparin contamination. | Review heparin exposure and ACT; consider protamine only if systemic heparin effect and clinical circumstances justify it, not solely because a contaminated sample was abnormal. |
| Rapid EXTEM clot breakdown; improves in APTEM | Hyperfibrinolysis may be contributing. | Consider TXA if appropriate for the setting and elapsed time; confirm the clinical context. A normal VEM does not exclude all forms of fibrinolytic disturbance. |

### Critically evaluate the available point-of-care tests

| **Test** | **Best clinical contribution** | **Limits worth stating in a viva** |
|---|---|---|
| ROTEM/TEG | Rapid global trends in clot initiation, firmness and lysis; targeted products; reassessment after each intervention. | Algorithms and thresholds differ by platform and local protocol; weak for some antiplatelet effects, vWD and endothelial disorders; temperature/pH of the tested sample may not reproduce in-vivo physiology. |
| ACT | Very rapid whole-blood anticoagulation measurement during high-dose heparin (CPB, selected interventional cases). | Affected by dilution, temperature, platelets and fibrinogen; not a reliable general coagulopathy or low-dose heparin assay. |
| Point-of-care Hb/Hct and blood gas | Track oxygen delivery, pH, potassium, ionised calcium, lactate and evolving dilution during major blood loss. | Hb can initially appear normal during acute haemorrhage; co-oximeter/POC Hb affected by sampling and fluid; no direct fibrinogen or platelet-function measurement. |
| Platelet-function analyser / aggregometry | Sometimes helps with suspected drug-related platelet inhibition or selected qualitative defects. | Not a standard standalone major-haemorrhage guide; tests are drug/platform-specific, require time or expertise and are influenced by platelet count/haematocrit. |

- Examiner calibration: the 2025.2 ANZCA SAQ required evaluation of a viscoelastic modality and at least one other POC modality, stating each test’s basis, advantages, limitations and clinical effect on rapid goal-directed decision-making.
- A description of ROTEM alone, however detailed, would not fully answer the question.
- Figures such as EXTEM CT >80–90 seconds, FIBTEM A5 <10 mm, or EXTEM A5 <35 mm occur in published Australian protocols, but thresholds vary between centres and devices.
- Quote one as a local example, not a universal definition.

## 4.3 A practical 10-minute loop for the anaesthetist

- **1.** **Identify the source and severity:** external blood, suction loss, surgical field, occult chest/abdominal/pelvic bleeding, obstetric source, trauma, vascular access or postoperative drain. Confirm ongoing haemorrhage, not only low BP from induction.
- **2.** **Control source:** direct pressure, packing, clamp, operative repair or urgent embolisation. Damage-control surgery and haemostatic resuscitation may be required when physiology is failing.
- **3.** **Resuscitate oxygen delivery:** oxygen/ventilation, temperature, large-bore access, appropriate RBCs and balanced components under MHP. Determine need for rapid transfuser or cell salvage.
- **4.** **Actively measure physiology:** arterial BP, gas/lactate, ionised Ca, temperature, haemoglobin and serial coagulation. Repeat testing at clinically useful intervals as volume and products change.
- **5.** **Target specific deficits:** fibrinogen first when low, platelets for low clot strength/count, plasma for multiple factor deficits, specific anticoagulant reversal when relevant, TXA when appropriately indicated.
- **6.** **Reassess for failure:** continued surgical bleeding despite corrected laboratory profile? Search for missed source. Normal coagulation tests do not mean definitive haemostasis.
- **7.** **Communicate transition:** stand down MHP when controlled, reconcile products, arrange monitored recovery and investigate delayed complications.

## 4.4 Trauma-induced coagulopathy versus dilutional and DIC mechanisms

- **Early trauma-induced coagulopathy (TIC)** is not simply a late result of massive transfusion.
- Tissue injury and shock drive endothelial injury, protein C-related pathways, fibrinolytic disturbances and platelet/factor dysfunction.
- Subsequent uncontrolled bleeding, cold crystalloid infusion, hypothermia, acidaemia and consumption make it worse.
- **Dilutional coagulopathy** develops after large-volume RBC/crystalloid without sufficient platelets/factors and can occur without a primary endothelial process.
- **DIC** is systemic thrombin generation from sepsis, malignancy, obstetric catastrophe or severe tissue injury, causing microthrombosis and consumption, with a variable bleeding phenotype.
- Distinguish them because the definitive treatment for TIC is bleeding control/resuscitation, for DIC is treatment of the driver, and for simple dilution is directed component repletion.

- In a trauma patient with uncontrolled bleeding, avoid unnecessary delay to surgery for ‘normalisation’ of coagulation labs.
- TXA is time-critical (within three hours if indicated).
- Permissive hypotension may be considered in selected uncontrolled haemorrhage without traumatic brain injury, but an injured brain needs adequate cerebral perfusion; do not use one BP target for all patients.
- Early pelvic binder, tourniquet and prompt surgical or interventional haemostasis are more important than any fashionable ratio.

## 4.5 Why massive transfusion itself causes complications

**Hypocalcaemia:**

- Citrate in blood components binds calcium, especially during rapid infusion or impaired hepatic metabolism; monitor ionised Ca, treat clinically important deficits with calcium chloride/gluconate per local protocol and venous access.
- Hypocalcaemia can worsen hypotension and clotting.
- **Hypothermia:** cold products and prolonged exposure reduce platelet/function and cause arrhythmias; use validated blood warmers.
- **Potassium abnormalities:** stored RBCs accumulate extracellular K, increasing hyperkalaemia risk during rapid transfusion, especially in neonates/renal dysfunction; later hypokalaemia can occur with restored metabolism and shifts.
- **Acid–base:** early shock acidosis, later citrate metabolism causing alkalosis; blood-product pH alone does not predict the patient’s acid-base state.

- **TACO / TRALI** can develop during or soon after resuscitation; differentiate when the patient develops pulmonary oedema.
- **Immunological complications:** haemolysis, allergic/anaphylactic reactions, alloimmunisation and delayed haemolysis.
- **Coagulopathy:** factor/platelet dilution, hypofibrinogenaemia, residual anticoagulants.
- **Infection** risk from modern screened components is much lower than historically but bacterial contamination (especially platelets) is important.
- **Other:** overload, increased exposure to donor products, metabolic complications, impaired microcirculation and resource errors.
- Prevention is not a single treatment: careful product checking, warmed balanced transfusion, frequent blood gas/iCa/coagulation reassessment, and early haemostasis are the bundle.

### Massive transfusion complications: recognise the mechanism and respond early

- Massive haemorrhage has two simultaneous problems: loss of circulating blood and loss of haemostatic function.
- The initial injury produces shock, endothelial damage and sometimes hyperfibrinolysis; aggressive resuscitation can then worsen dilution, hypothermia and biochemical disturbance.
- In a viva, prevention should begin at MHP activation—not when a cardiac arrhythmia or diffuse surgical ooze appears.

| **Problem** | **Mechanism and bedside clues** | **Prevention and treatment** |
|---|---|---|
| Citrate-associated hypocalcaemia ± hypomagnesaemia | Citrate chelates ionised calcium and magnesium. Rapid component infusion, hypoperfusion and impaired hepatic metabolism increase risk; may cause hypotension, weak contractility, prolonged QT or arrhythmia. | Frequent ionised Ca (often with blood gas); titrated IV calcium chloride or gluconate, checking line suitability and response. Maintain physiological Ca rather than treating only total calcium; check Mg. |
| Hyperkalaemia → later hypokalaemia | Stored RBC extracellular potassium can rise during storage; rapid delivery/older or irradiated units and renal impairment increase risk, especially in paediatrics. With recovery of perfusion and catecholamines, hypokalaemia can follow. | Serial K and ECG; stabilise membrane with calcium and shift K intracellularly if severe; avoid indiscriminate K replacement before trends are known. |
| Hypothermia | Unwarmed blood and exposed surgical surfaces impair platelet function and coagulation enzyme kinetics, worsen acidosis and dysrhythmias. | Blood/IV fluid warmer, forced-air warming and core temperature monitoring. Correct with active warming alongside haemostasis, not after bleeding stops. |
| Dilutional/consumptive coagulopathy | Loss and dilution of platelets, fibrinogen and factors plus TIC/DIC, acidosis and hypothermia. Fibrinogen may fall early. | Source control; MHP with early components; serial platelets/PT/APTT/fibrinogen and VEM; directed fibrinogen/platelet/plasma replacement. |
| Acidosis, hypoperfusion and reperfusion | Low flow causes lactate and reduces coagulation and myocardial performance; citrate metabolism and reperfusion can alter acid–base status. | Restore circulation/source control and oxygen delivery. Correct cause first; bicarbonate does not substitute for perfusion; trend ABG/lactate. |
| TACO, TRALI, haemolysis or incompatibility | High infusion volumes can cause hydrostatic pulmonary oedema; TRALI causes permeability oedema; clerical incompatibility causes haemolysis/DIC. | Reassess volume status and oxygenation, maintain bedside identifiers and blood-bank communication; stop suspected reaction immediately and investigate (Chapter 9). |
| Alloimmunisation / delayed haemolysis / iron loading | Repeated donor exposure can form red-cell alloantibodies and make future crossmatching difficult; chronic heavy exposure causes iron accumulation. | Use PBM, correct product selection, clear transfusion history and follow-up if delayed Hb fall/jaundice. Iron overload matters in chronic transfusion, less in one MHP. |

- Suggested monitoring loop in ongoing critical bleeding: repeat ABG with ionised calcium, potassium, glucose, pH and lactate; FBC/platelets, PT/APTT, fibrinogen and VEM according to severity, often every 20–30 minutes during uncontrolled haemorrhage rather than at fixed intervals after bleeding stops.
- Review core temperature, rhythm, urine output, blood loss, products given and surgical haemostasis.
- Use local MHP thresholds and reassess after each targeted intervention; haemostatic product selection should reflect the actual deficit.

items.title: 5. Rational blood-component therapy in theatre and ICU
items.body:
## 5.1 The central decision: what deficit is being treated?

- Transfuse only when the anticipated benefit of a specific component exceeds its immediate and longer-term risks.
- For RBCs the immediate purpose is to improve **oxygen-carrying capacity**, not to expand circulating volume in a haemodynamically stable patient.
- For plasma the purpose is factor replacement; for platelets, platelet number/function; for cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate, polymerisable fibrin formation.
- Each has different indications and does **not** substitute for treating the cause of loss.
- In critical bleeding, components may be needed before testing returns; in the stable ICU patient, a slower targeted approach reduces unnecessary exposure.

### Packed red cells

- A standard adult RBC unit usually increases Hb by roughly 10 g/L in an average nonbleeding adult, although body size, haemolysis, fluid shifts and continuing loss alter the response.
- Modern leukodepleted units reduce febrile reactions, CMV-related transmission risk and some alloimmunisation, but do not eliminate all transfusion hazards.
- Obtain the appropriate ABO/Rh-compatible or emergency-release product, verify the patient and product at the bedside, and monitor clinical response.
- Do not use ‘one unit raises Hb 10’ as a resuscitation calculation during active haemorrhage.

**Thresholds (2023 AABB; stable adults):**

- Consider transfusion when Hb **<70 g/L** for most haemodynamically stable hospitalised adults and many stable ICU patients.
- A threshold around **75 g/L** may be chosen for cardiac surgery and **80 g/L** for major orthopaedic surgery or pre-existing cardiovascular disease, in keeping with trial populations.
- These are consideration thresholds, not mandatory transfusion targets.
- Symptoms of anaemia, ischaemia, impaired oxygen delivery, active loss and patient-specific reserve matter.
- **Acute MI/ACS is a distinct situation:** MINT suggests possible benefit of a more liberal approach toward 100 g/L, and contemporary ACS guidance is more permissive, so do not automatically apply the general ICU 70 g/L threshold in active infarction.
- **During ongoing exsanguination, a fixed Hb trigger is inappropriate.**

After each RBC unit in a stable nonbleeding patient, reassess symptoms, perfusion and Hb rather than automatically ordering two units. A ‘normal’ postoperative Hb is not required for safe discharge if the patient is stable and the cause is addressed.

### Plasma, platelets and fibrinogen

| **Product** | **Principal contents / purpose** | **Appropriate use** | **Not appropriate as routine use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) | Soluble clotting factors including V, VII, VIII and fibrinogen in relatively low concentration | Significant factor deficiency with active bleeding, urgent procedure when specific therapy unavailable, component of critical bleeding MHP | Routine volume expansion, isolated minor INR prolongation without bleeding, nutrition |
| Platelets | Platelet dose for primary haemostasis | Active bleeding with low count/function, prevention at critical procedural thresholds, selected intracranial/critical-site bleeding | Correcting a mildly low count without risk; prophylactic platelet transfusion in HIT/TTP without serious bleeding |
| Cryoprecipitate | Fibrinogen-rich fraction with VIII, XIII, vWF | Low fibrinogen in bleeding/procedural patient; DIC/obstetric/trauma contexts | Generic reversal of all anticoagulants |
| Fibrinogen concentrate | Standardised fibrinogen dose, small volume | Acquired fibrinogen deficiency under local bleeding protocols; selected congenital deficiencies | Substitute for platelets or clotting factors when those are the deficits |
| Four-factor PCC | Factors II, VII, IX, X (and variable proteins C/S) | Rapid warfarin reversal in life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery | Generic volume resuscitation or routine factor replacement with normal vitamin K factors |
| Specific concentrates | vWF, FVIII/IX, FXIII etc. | Known factor deficiency or acquired inhibitor under haematology plan | Empirical treatment of every prolonged APTT |

**Plasma dose:**

- Often 10–15 mL/kg in bleeding factor deficiency, adjusted to measured response, product and protocol.
- In a nonbleeding patient with mildly prolonged INR, small plasma doses are unlikely to change haemostasis meaningfully and can cause TACO.
- **Platelet thresholds** are clinical: prophylaxis commonly considered below 10 ×10⁹/L for stable chemotherapy-related marrow suppression, higher with fever/other risks; ≈50 ×10⁹/L for significant active bleeding or many invasive procedures and ≈100 ×10⁹/L for intracranial/neurosurgical bleeding.
- These are guides, not substitutes for procedural guidance, platelet function or diagnosis (e.g. TTP/HIT).
- Do not transfuse prophylactic platelets merely because counts are low in DIC when no bleeding/procedure is planned, unless there is an exceptional context.

### Practical management when the blood bank cannot immediately supply compatible RBCs

- Occult alloantibodies or rare phenotypes can delay compatible blood during life-threatening haemorrhage.
- The initial clinical priority remains haemostasis and oxygen delivery.
- Contact a senior transfusion scientist and haematologist early; identify known historical antibodies and whether emergency uncrossmatched group O RBCs are necessary.
- Transfusion-associated risk must be clearly communicated and documented; crossmatched antigen-negative blood should replace emergency issue as soon as feasible.
- In a patient with known warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, pan-reactive crossmatch may make ‘fully compatible’ RBC selection impossible; seek specialist selection that excludes clinically significant alloantibodies rather than withholding lifesaving transfusion until all reactivity disappears.
- In a pregnant patient or one with childbearing potential, RhD/Kell considerations matter for future alloimmunisation, but imminent death from exsanguination overrides attempts to achieve ideal matched stock when none is available.

### Component decisions that are frequently answered poorly

- **A stable patient with INR 1.5 scheduled for central venous access** rarely benefits from prophylactic FFP; procedural technique, ultrasound and compressibility matter, and volume loading from plasma can be harmful.
- The specific coagulation disorder and procedural risk must be considered.
- **A nonbleeding chemotherapy patient with platelets 8 ×10⁹/L** generally warrants prophylactic platelets, unlike **a stable consumptive thrombocytopenia patient with platelets 65 ×10⁹/L**, where treatment of sepsis and daily trends may be appropriate without any platelet transfusion.
- **A platelet count of 110 ×10⁹/L on aspirin does not automatically justify platelets before cardiac surgery**; bleeding, surgery type and evidence of clinically relevant dysfunction decide.
- In spontaneous nonoperative intracranial bleeding with platelet count >100 ×10⁹/L, 2025 AABB/ICTMG guidance recommends against routine platelet transfusion solely for antiplatelet exposure; operative neurosurgical circumstances require separate discussion.

- **Fibrinogen kinetics** help explain why a normal INR can coexist with severe coagulopathic bleeding.
- Fibrinogen is often the first coagulation substrate to reach a critically low concentration during extensive haemorrhage or severe obstetric bleeding.
- Replacing it with FFP alone requires large volumes; cryoprecipitate or concentrate delivers fibrinogen more efficiently.
- On the other hand, fibrinogen is an acute-phase reactant and may remain high in early septic DIC; high fibrinogen does not exclude pathological coagulation activation.
- Finally, **platelet function** may be poor despite normal count after CPB, uraemia or potent antiplatelet treatment: numbers alone do not tell the whole story.

- **Desmopressin (DDAVP)** releases endothelial vWF/FVIII and can transiently improve platelet adhesion in selected uraemic bleeding, mild haemophilia A or vWD; it is not a general reversal agent for all bleeding.
- A common haemostatic dose is 0.3 μg/kg IV over 20–30 minutes where indicated, with fluid restriction/sodium monitoring because hyponatraemia and tachyphylaxis can occur.
- **Recombinant activated factor VII** is not routine rescue for uncontrolled surgical haemorrhage: potential thrombotic harms and limited outcome evidence mean it should only be considered after source control, correction of substrate and specialist review in exceptional cases.

## 5.2 Applying the restrictive strategy in ICU

- Anaemia of critical illness is multifactorial: haemodilution, repeated sampling, inflammation-mediated iron restriction, blunted erythropoietin response, haemolysis, renal disease and occult bleeding.
- Treatment begins by determining the cause.
- Stable septic-shock patients usually do not benefit from routinely maintaining Hb around 90–100 g/L; **TRISS** found similar mortality with restrictive and liberal triggers.
- **TRICC** established that restrictive transfusion is safe for many stable critically ill adults, but its broad message should not be extrapolated without thought to active MI, ongoing haemorrhage or selected neurocritical states.
- **TRICS III** supports restrictive strategies in cardiac surgery.
- The relevant outcome is patient-centred benefit, not achieving a reassuring number.

- **Specific ICU contexts:**

- **Sepsis without active haemorrhage:** consider Hb <70 g/L unless myocardial ischaemia, severe hypoxaemia or ongoing bleeding modifies threshold; treat perfusion, oxygenation and infection first.
- **Acute MI/ACS:** balance ischaemic oxygen demand against TACO and transfusion harm; individualise, consider more liberal strategy in light of MINT and current ACS guidance.
- **Traumatic brain injury:** evaluate cerebral oxygen delivery, bleeding and risk; the HEMOTION trial did not conclusively demonstrate superiority of a liberal strategy for its primary endpoint, but clinically important uncertainty remains. A generic 70 g/L recommendation for every severe TBI patient is too strong.
- **Haematological malignancy:** restrictive RBC threshold around 70 g/L is supported with lower-certainty evidence, but marrow failure, disease-directed targets, symptoms, bleeding and transplant requirements are relevant.
- **ECMO/CPB or advanced circulatory support:** perfusion/oxygen delivery, flow and specific protocol matter; do not automatically use arbitrary historical ‘Hb 100’ targets.

### Why don’t we automatically transfuse to 100 g/L?

- Allogeneic RBCs increase oxygen content but do not necessarily correct cellular oxygen extraction, microcirculatory shunting or primary shock.
- RBC transfusion can worsen fluid overload, inflammation and circulatory stress.
- The improvement in Hb must be weighed against transfusion complications.
- Critically evaluate the clinical **indication**, alternative treatments, and whether the patient has sufficient cardiopulmonary reserve; use blood components to treat a specific deficit.

## 5.3 Special blood-bank planning

- **ABO compatibility** is critical to avoid immediate intravascular haemolysis.
- For RBCs, O-negative is commonly used when compatible typed blood is unavailable, with stewardship and transition to group-specific products when safe; group-specific RBCs may follow validated emergency group checks.
- Plasma compatibility runs in the opposite direction because donor antibodies must not attack recipient RBCs; AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B but group-specific alternatives may be used in emergency protocols.
- **RhD** particularly matters for people of childbearing potential; immunoglobulin and product strategies are patient-specific.
- Document pre-existing alloantibodies (e.g. anti-K, anti-E), pregnancy history and transfusion reactions.
- Certain groups require **irradiated** cellular components to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (not simply every malignancy patient).
- **CMV-safe** and other modifications depend on indication/local policy.
- **Washed components** may help repeated severe allergy.
- Leucoreduction is not equivalent to irradiation.

### Storage lesion and ‘fresh blood’

- During RBC storage, extracellular potassium rises, 2,3-DPG initially falls, membrane changes occur and free haemoglobin/microparticles accumulate.
- Most adult RCT evidence does not support routinely selecting ‘fresh’ versus standard-issue RBCs to improve major outcomes.
- Small children, high-volume rapid transfusion, exchange transfusion and special circumstances can require tailored product selection.
- Fresh frozen plasma and platelets have their own storage/transport rules; know your blood service’s expiry, warming and administration policies.

items.title: 6. Thromboembolic disease and anticoagulation in the perioperative ICU
items.body:
## 6.1 Why surgery produces thrombosis

- VTE arises from Virchow’s triad: **venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability**.
- Surgery provides tissue injury and inflammation; anaesthesia, immobility and critical illness reduce flow; infection, malignancy, trauma, pregnancy, oestrogen therapy and inherited thrombophilia may increase coagulation.
- A previous unprovoked VTE or active malignancy usually matters far more than an isolated mild laboratory abnormality.
- VTE can cause limb symptoms, PE with RV failure or death, and long-term post-thrombotic syndrome/chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

**Risk factors:**

- Prior VTE, active cancer, older age, obesity, immobility, major pelvic/abdominal/orthopaedic surgery, trauma, ICU stay, inflammatory disease, pregnancy/postpartum, OCP/HRT, strong thrombophilia, central venous catheters and acute infection.
- Risk assessment models (e.g. Caprini in some surgical pathways) help organise risk but have limitations and must be applied with procedure-specific guidance.
- **Bleeding risk** (ongoing haemorrhage, recent intracranial bleeding, unstable haemostasis, severe thrombocytopenia, spinal/epidural procedures) must be assessed simultaneously.

## 6.2 Prevention: mechanical, pharmacological and mobilisation

- Early mobilisation and hydration are helpful but not adequate prophylaxis for many high-risk surgical patients.
- Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) reduces venous stasis without pharmacological bleeding risk; it is particularly valuable immediately when anticoagulants are temporarily unsafe.
- Stockings are less favoured than IPC in many guidelines.
- Pharmacological prophylaxis usually uses **LMWH or low-dose UFH**, modified for renal failure, weight, HIT, bleeding and neuraxial procedures.
- Selected orthopaedic protocols use DOACs or aspirin; the appropriate choice is surgery-specific, not universal.

- For **high VTE risk with acceptable bleeding risk**, combining IPC with anticoagulant prophylaxis can be appropriate.
- For **high bleeding risk**, IPC first and commence anticoagulants once haemostasis is secure.
- Extended prophylaxis (often ≈28 days) is appropriate after certain high-risk cancer abdominal/pelvic operations and selected major orthopaedic surgery; it is not necessary after every minor operation.
- Prophylactic IVC filters are generally not recommended.
- The 2019 ASH surgical VTE guideline provides a useful framework, but the patient’s own risk, local policy and the surgeon’s understanding of haemostasis remain crucial.

## 6.3 Suspected DVT/PE in the perioperative setting

**DVT:**

- New unilateral swelling/pain, proximal venous tenderness and asymmetric oedema are suggestive but nonspecific.
- Use clinical probability and compression ultrasound.
- D-dimer is frequently elevated after major surgery, trauma, malignancy or infection and cannot be used indiscriminately to diagnose postoperative DVT.
- **PE:** unexplained tachycardia, hypoxaemia, pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, collapse or falling ETCO₂ under anaesthesia; massive PE may present as acute RV failure with hypotension.
- Perform CTPA in stable patients when appropriate; bedside focused echo and compression ultrasound may guide urgent decisions in unstable patients unable to travel.
- Absence of RV dilation does not exclude PE.

- **Initial management** prioritises oxygenation, RV perfusion, avoidance of hypoxaemia/hypercapnia/acidosis and anticoagulation when indicated/feasible.
- UFH infusion offers short half-life and rapid interruption in unstable patients needing invasive procedures or with high bleeding risk; LMWH/DOACs suit selected stable patients.
- **Haemodynamically high-risk PE** may require systemic thrombolysis, catheter intervention or embolectomy.
- Recent major surgery is a substantial bleeding contraindication to systemic lysis, so urgent multidisciplinary PE-team assessment is vital.
- An IVC filter is a limited exception when acute proximal DVT/PE coexists with a true contraindication to anticoagulation; retrieve when feasible rather than leaving it indefinitely.

## 6.4 Therapeutic anticoagulation in ICU

- **UFH** is useful in unstable patients, severe renal impairment and situations likely to need urgent procedures; infusion monitoring is via APTT or anti-Xa according to local assay and clinical context.
- Heparin resistance can arise from antithrombin deficiency, acute-phase proteins or assay interference; blindly escalating based on an APTT alone risks overdose.
- **LMWH** offers predictable effect and lower HIT risk, but accumulates with renal dysfunction and may require dose adjustment/monitoring.
- **DOACs** have important interactions, depend on renal/hepatic function and oral absorption, and may be inappropriate in shock or when enteral absorption is uncertain.
- **Warfarin** remains important for mechanical valves and selected contexts; bridge only when thrombotic risk justifies it rather than automatically.

### Anticoagulant interruption, reversal and restart

- **Warfarin:** four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K for life-threatening bleeding/urgent reversal, guided by INR, weight and local protocol; PCC acts rapidly but vitamin K provides sustained correction. Small vitamin K alone is too slow for active exsanguination.
- **Dabigatran:** idarucizumab 5 g IV (given as two 2.5 g doses) for qualifying life-threatening bleeding/urgent surgery; adjust definitive management for renal function and rebound levels.
- **Factor Xa inhibitors:** andexanet alfa has specific indications and availability limitations; some centres use four-factor PCC for selected critical bleeding. Haematology advice and current institutional availability are essential; routine reversal of non-life-threatening bleeding is inappropriate.
- **UFH:** protamine, typically approximately 1 mg per 100 units recently infused (maximum/infusion rate per protocol), reducing dose for elapsed time; avoid hypotension/anaphylactoid effects.
- **LMWH:** protamine partially reverses, especially anti-IIa effect, but not all anti-Xa activity; seek specialist advice.
- **Antiplatelet drugs:** platelet transfusion is not routine prophylactic reversal; case-dependent severe bleeding, ticagrelor persistence, neurosurgery and agent-specific issues need specialist discussion.

- Restart requires demonstrated haemostasis and a plan for prophylaxis versus therapeutic treatment.
- A stable patient after low-risk surgery may restart sooner than a patient after major intracranial, spinal or gastrointestinal bleeding.
- Indwelling neuraxial catheters impose independent timing constraints: **the 2025 ASRA fifth edition differentiates low-dose from high-dose DOACs** (e.g. high-dose apixaban commonly requires ≥72 h before neuraxial/deep plexus block; low-dose apixaban ≥36 h), but timing also depends on kidney function and catheter removal, and local 2026 ANZCA guidance should be checked.
- Do not treat a patient’s last dose alone as proof of neuraxial safety.

### Three perioperative anticoagulation scenarios that illustrate the decision

**Scenario A: AF on apixaban requiring elective colectomy:**
