- First determine stroke risk, renal function, dose, last administration and surgical bleeding risk.
- In many patients a standard short DOAC interruption without bridging is appropriate (PAUSE), with restart after established postoperative haemostasis.
- A typical high-bleeding-risk surgical interruption might involve holding approximately two days before the operation and restarting 48–72 h later if haemostasis is secure; the exact recommendation varies by product, kidney function and procedure.
- If the surgeon proposes a thoracic epidural, this changes the plan: high-dose apixaban usually requires at least 72 h before neuraxial/deep plexus block under 2025 ASRA, with separate catheter-removal and restart intervals.
- Do not infer neuraxial safety from a generic two-day surgical withholding policy.

**Scenario B: mechanical mitral valve on warfarin requiring urgent surgery:**

- The risk of thrombosis is materially higher than uncomplicated AF, especially with previous valve thrombosis/embolism or older prostheses.
- Determine actual INR, urgency and bleeding risk.
- In life-threatening haemorrhage or surgery unable to wait for INR normalisation, give four-factor PCC and IV vitamin K as appropriate; factor replacement corrects INR rapidly whereas vitamin K makes it durable.
- A planned heparin bridge during an elective interruption is a specialist decision, not a universal rule: CHEST 2022 generally suggests against routine bridging even in mechanical valves, while valve/perioperative guidance reserves consideration for particularly high-risk valves.
- Reintroduce warfarin and, if indicated, therapeutic heparin only after adequate haemostasis, allowing for procedure and any neuraxial catheter.
- Heparin in the same time window as epidural insertion/removal carries spinal haematoma risk.

- **Scenario C: therapeutic LMWH for PE diagnosed two weeks ago, now urgent abdominal surgery.** Recent PE confers high recurrent thrombosis risk; postponement is preferred if clinically possible.
- If urgent, assess PE severity/RV function, bleeding risk, last LMWH dose, renal function and whether UFH’s short half-life would be more controllable.
- Avoid a blanket ‘48 h hold’ based solely on agent name.
- Plan mechanical prophylaxis during unsafe anticoagulant windows, restart prophylactic/therapeutic regimens in stages if haemostasis permits, and discuss exceptional filter use only when a genuine prolonged contraindication to anticoagulation exists.
- Active DVT/PE is not cured by inserting an IVC filter.

**Dose versus drug level:**

- Standard PT/INR and APTT cannot reliably exclude clinically relevant apixaban/rivaroxaban activity.
- Where urgent procedures make the decision borderline, a drug-calibrated anti-Xa assay or appropriate dabigatran test may help.
- Results depend on time since dose, specimen handling and assay availability.
- Reversing an anticoagulant can increase thrombotic risk; reserve specific reversal for life-threatening bleeding or truly urgent procedures that cannot safely wait.
- Routine reversal solely to permit elective neuraxial anaesthesia is not recommended.

### Differentiate preventive doses from treatment of established thrombosis

- The clinical question changes completely once thrombosis is proven.
- Prophylactic-dose LMWH/UFH aims to prevent a first VTE in an immobilised or high-risk patient; it does not treat confirmed proximal DVT or PE.
- Therapeutic anticoagulation requires weight/organ-function appropriate dosing, bleeding assessment and a follow-up duration plan.
- In an ICU patient with ongoing bleeding, use mechanical prophylaxis while anticoagulation is genuinely contraindicated, and reassess that contraindication at least daily rather than allowing prophylaxis to be omitted indefinitely.

| **Setting** | **Default reasoning** | **Important exception or escalation** |
|---|---|---|
| Stable proximal DVT or non-high-risk PE | Therapeutic anticoagulation if bleeding risk acceptable; evaluate renal function, invasive procedures, malignancy, pregnancy, interactions and drug absorption. DOAC often suits a stable ambulant patient; UFH may suit unstable ICU/anticipated procedures. | Treat an acute provoked event for an initial minimum of about 3 months; 2026 PE guidance frames the initial phase as 3–6 months according to patient factors. Active cancer or persistent risks may warrant longer; reassess bleeding and recurrence. |
| High-risk PE: shock or persistent haemodynamic compromise | Resuscitate RV failure, oxygenation and coronary/RV perfusion, urgent bedside echo/CT when feasible; initiate UFH if safe and organise reperfusion assessment with PE team. | Recent major surgery may prohibit systemic thrombolysis. Consider catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy, or rescue ECMO in selected centres, balancing bleeding. |
| Acute limb ischaemia / arterial embolus | A different vascular emergency: six Ps, threatened limb, pulses and Doppler; urgent vascular surgeon, IV UFH if no contraindication while planning revascularisation. | Do not confuse with DVT or defer limb-saving treatment for a routine thrombophilia work-up. Monitor reperfusion acidosis, hyperkalaemia and compartment syndrome. |
| Extracorporeal circuit thrombosis | Investigate anticoagulation interruption, access/flow problems, filter characteristics, platelet counts and HIT. | Circuit anticoagulation is not synonymous with systemic VTE treatment. Citrate CRRT provides circuit protection without providing therapeutic systemic anticoagulation. |

- Do not insert an inferior vena cava filter routinely in a patient who can receive anticoagulation.
- A retrievable filter is a selectively reasonable bridge in acute proximal DVT/PE with an absolute temporary contraindication to therapeutic anticoagulation; document a removal plan once anticoagulation becomes safe.
- The filter itself can cause DVT/caval complications and does not treat the existing clot.
- In very recent VTE (especially <3 months), elective major surgery should be postponed where possible; if it cannot be postponed, record a multidisciplinary plan covering anticoagulant interruption, bleeding rescue and early restart.

### What changes anticoagulant monitoring in the critically ill?

- UFH: titrate using locally validated APTT or anti-Xa.
- APTT may be misleading with high factor VIII/fibrinogen (acute inflammation), lupus anticoagulant, factor deficiency or haemodilution; anti-Xa can be more informative in selected heparin resistance/discordance cases.
- LMWH: renal clearance makes accumulation possible at low creatinine clearance; assess dose and whether anti-Xa monitoring or UFH is more suitable.
- DOACs: altered enteral absorption, acute kidney injury, liver dysfunction and interactions can make ICU use less predictable; PT/APTT are not reliable rule-out tests for residual drug effect.
- Warfarin: INR monitoring and interactions are especially important with sepsis, antibiotics and variable nutrition.
- Therapeutic anticoagulation cannot be assumed safe for a neuraxial catheter solely because the surgical wound appears dry.

## 6.5 Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

- HIT is an **immune prothrombotic syndrome** in which IgG against platelet factor 4/heparin complexes activates platelets and generates thrombin.
- Platelet count usually falls >50% around day 5–10 after exposure, or earlier with recent heparin re-exposure.
- Thrombosis (venous/arterial), skin necrosis and circuit clotting can occur even though the platelet count is low.
- It is distinct from mild early nonimmune heparin-associated thrombocytopenia.

- **Assess 4Ts score** (degree of thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis and other causes); low scores make HIT unlikely and avoid unnecessary immunoassays.
- With intermediate/high probability: **stop all heparin including line flushes**, send PF4 immunoassay with confirmatory functional assay where indicated, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant if bleeding risk permits (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC depending on stability, organ function and local advice).
- Do **not** start warfarin acutely before platelet recovery because of risk of venous limb gangrene/skin necrosis; reverse warfarin if started in acute HIT after specialist review.
- Platelet transfusion is usually avoided except for serious bleeding or urgent intervention.

## 6.6 Anticoagulation in organ support

**CRRT:**

- Regional citrate anticoagulation is often preferred where available because it anticoagulates the circuit without systemic heparin exposure; monitor systemic/circuit ionised calcium, total:iCa ratio, acid-base and citrate accumulation risk (shock/severe hepatic dysfunction may impair metabolism).
- UFH is an option, but bleeding/HIT risk matters.
- **ECMO:** unfractionated heparin is common, with anti-Xa/APTT/ACT or other monitoring as centre-specific; the balance of circuit thrombosis, intracranial bleeding and acquired vWF changes is complex.
- Avoid equating a normal APTT with adequate ECMO anticoagulation or excluding bleeding risk.
- **Arterial thrombosis** (acute limb ischaemia, vascular devices) requires urgent vascular assessment, anticoagulation and reperfusion where indicated rather than waiting for routine VTE pathways.

items.title: 7. Coagulopathy in intensive care: DIC and major mimics
items.body:
## 7.1 DIC is a syndrome, not a laboratory diagnosis in isolation

- DIC is systemic activation of coagulation from an underlying process causing diffuse microvascular fibrin deposition, consumption of platelets/factors and abnormal fibrinolysis.
- **Sepsis** often produces a thrombotic phenotype with suppressed fibrinolysis and organ failure; **obstetric catastrophe, trauma, leukaemia** may produce dramatic bleeding with high fibrinolytic activity.
- The clinical spectrum spans thrombosis to severe bleeding; a patient may have both at once.

**Common triggers:**

- Sepsis, shock, severe trauma, placental abruption/amniotic-fluid embolism/retained stillbirth, metastatic cancer, acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), vascular malformations, pancreatitis, snake envenoming and major transfusion.
- Do not label every ICU thrombocytopenia as DIC: think dilution, drugs, HIT, TTP/HUS, liver dysfunction, marrow failure and sepsis-related platelet consumption.

### Diagnostic approach

- **1.** Assess source, acute changes, organ dysfunction, bleeding, purpura or limb ischaemia.
- **2.** Serial **platelets** (falling), **PT** (prolonging), **fibrinogen** (may fall, but can be normal/high early in inflammatory sepsis), **D-dimer/FDP** (often raised) and blood film.
- **3.** Apply the **ISTH overt-DIC score** where useful: platelet count (<100 or <50), elevated fibrin markers (moderate/strong), PT prolongation (3–6 s or >6 s), and low fibrinogen (<1 g/L); a score ≥5 supports overt DIC in a patient with an appropriate underlying disorder.
  - Not a substitute for bedside diagnosis; repeat as disease evolves.
- **4.** Assess renal, hepatic, neurological and respiratory injury; look for a driver such as infection or malignancy. DIC is a dynamic process and scores based on single samples can be misleading.

| **Disorder** | **Clue distinguishing it from DIC** | **Why management differs** |
|---|---|---|
| Severe liver disease | Chronic derangement, low synthetic capacity; INR not a global bleeding test | Rebalanced haemostasis; avoid reflex plasma correction without bleeding |
| TTP | Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, severe thrombocytopenia, often relatively normal PT/APTT; ADAMTS13 severe deficiency | Urgent plasma exchange/caplacizumab specialist protocol; avoid routine platelets |
| HUS | MAHA, AKI, diarrhoeal or complement-mediated trigger | Supportive/targeted management; specific complement therapy in selected cases |
| HIT | 5–10 d after heparin, >50% platelet fall, new thrombosis, PT/APTT often otherwise unremarkable | Stop heparin/start alternative anticoagulant |
| Vitamin K deficiency / warfarin | Disproportionate PT/INR increase, nutritional/drug history | Vitamin K/PCC when indicated |
| Dilutional coagulopathy | Large-volume resuscitation/CPB, falling fibrinogen/platelets | Stop bleeding, targeted factor and platelet replacement |

### Interpret a deteriorating DIC patient step by step

- A patient with septic shock develops an abrupt platelet fall, worsening renal function, mottled extremities and prolonged PT.
- At this stage determine whether organ dysfunction is from septic microvascular thrombosis, ongoing shock, a drug toxicity, HIT or a thrombotic microangiopathy.
- Request a film and haemolysis panel if schistocytes/MAHA are suspected; review heparin timing; look for infection source and cultures.
- If the patient is not actively bleeding, random plasma and platelets may not improve outcomes and can increase TACO/ARDS risk.
- Continue treatment of sepsis, organ support and appropriately selected thromboprophylaxis.
- If laparotomy becomes urgent with diffuse bleeding, **the clinical indication has changed:** targeted platelets, fibrinogen and plasma may now be needed for haemostasis, alongside source control.

- An APL patient may also have a low platelet count and fibrinogen but requires a different intervention: immediate haematology-led ATRA and intensive haemostatic support because catastrophic intracranial or pulmonary haemorrhage can occur early.
- The same laboratory pattern can therefore signal different diseases and different definitive treatments.
- For TTP, however, platelet transfusion may accelerate microthrombosis; unless life-threatening bleeding requires it, the urgent treatment is plasma exchange and specialist TTP therapy.
- These differences are why coagulopathy management must start with **cause + clinical phenotype**, not an isolated INR or platelet threshold.

## 7.2 Treat the disease first, not the INR

**Definitive treatment is control of the driver:**

- Antibiotics/source control in sepsis, delivery/haemostasis in obstetric DIC, early ATRA in APL, appropriate cancer treatment or surgery for vascular catastrophe.
- In a nonbleeding patient with DIC and no procedure, prophylactic plasma is usually not beneficial and may worsen fluid overload.
- In major bleeding or procedures, give fibrinogen replacement when low, platelets when indicated (commonly target >50 ×10⁹/L for active bleeding), and FFP for significant multiple factor deficits; use clinical context and available laboratory/VEM guidance.
- If thrombosis dominates, pharmacological VTE prophylaxis or full anticoagulation may be appropriate under specialist advice despite thrombocytopenia.
- The mere diagnosis of DIC does not universally prohibit heparin.

### Acquired factor inhibitors and uncommon dangerous diagnoses

- **Acquired haemophilia A** can present with spontaneous severe soft-tissue/GI/postoperative bleeding, no prior history, isolated prolonged APTT and failure of correction on mixing (sometimes time-dependent).
- Management is haemostatic bypassing agents/recombinant porcine VIII according to specialists plus immunosuppression to eradicate inhibitor; do not rely on FFP as definitive therapy.
- **APL-associated coagulopathy** frequently causes severe early bleeding and requires urgent ATRA before full confirmation when suspected plus aggressive supportive fibrinogen/platelet maintenance.
- **Severe acquired vWF deficiency** may follow aortic stenosis, ECMO or mechanical circulatory support; platelet count may be normal despite mucosal bleeding.

### Distinguish consumptive bleeding after trauma, sepsis and liver failure

- A practical case: a septic laparotomy patient develops platelet decline from 180 to 55 ×10⁹/L, INR 1.8, fibrinogen 3.5 g/L, and dusky fingers.
- This can represent **thrombotic sepsis-associated coagulopathy** despite preserved/high fibrinogen because inflammatory hepatic synthesis masks consumption.
- If bleeding is absent, giving several units of FFP to normalise INR does not address microvascular thrombin generation and may cause fluid overload.
- Treat infection/source and maintain tissue perfusion, repeat measurements, assess microthrombosis, and give pharmacological VTE prevention once safely indicated.
- Contrast with placental abruption/obstetric DIC, where fibrinogen can fall rapidly and diffuse bleeding requires immediate replacement while controlling the obstetric cause.
- Contrast also with decompensated cirrhosis, where low procoagulants coexist with low anticoagulant proteins and increased vWF—INR is not equivalent to total bleeding risk.
- In a cirrhotic patient with active major bleeding, direct haemostasis, platelets/fibrinogen and portal-hypertensive mechanisms matter more than restoring INR to 1.0.

items.title: 8. Anaemia and thrombocytopenia in intensive care
items.body:
## 8.1 Anaemia: classify by mechanism, not only MCV

- The ICU patient commonly has impaired erythropoiesis, hepcidin-mediated functional iron deficiency, haemodilution and iatrogenic sampling.
- Begin with **trend and reticulocyte response**.
- A high reticulocyte count suggests loss or destruction; inadequate reticulocytes suggest marrow suppression, inflammation, nutritional deficit or renal failure.
- Iron indices require interpretation with inflammation; low ferritin remains helpful, but normal/high ferritin does not exclude functional deficiency.
- Investigate bleeding, haemolysis (LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, film), infection and drug effects.
- In the stable patient, treat deficiencies and reduce phlebotomy rather than repeated RBC transfusion with no durable strategy.
- ESA therapy is not routine for general ICU anaemia owing to modest benefits and thrombosis risk.

- **Anaemia in a patient with renal dysfunction** may reflect reduced EPO but also bleeding, haemolysis or inflammation.
- **After CPB** consider surgical loss, haemodilution, haemolysis and chest drain loss.
- **With unexplained falling Hb and normal drains**, suspect retroperitoneal/occult haemorrhage, repeated diagnostic blood loss or haemolysis.
- Every low Hb deserves a physiological assessment: is there impaired delivery, continuing loss, myocardial ischaemia or merely reduced concentration after fluid?

## 8.2 Thrombocytopenia: five questions at the bedside

- **1.** **Is the count real?** Review film and repeat citrate sample if platelet clumps.
- **2.** **When did it fall?** Admission, day 1 after CPB, day 5–10 heparin exposure or after new antibiotic.
- **3.** **Is there bleeding or thrombosis?** Look for petechiae, surgical ooze, purpura, DVT or circuit thrombosis.
- **4.** **Are other cells affected?** Pancytopenia suggests marrow disorder; schistocytes + haemolysis suggests TMA.
- **5.** **Is an intervention pending?** Procedural target and functional risk determine transfusion, not count alone.

- **Mechanisms:** decreased production (marrow suppression, chemotherapy, sepsis, malignancy), increased destruction/consumption (sepsis, DIC, HIT, ITP, TTP/HUS), sequestration (splenomegaly), dilution and artefact. Examine medication exposure (heparin, quinine, vancomycin, linezolid and others), circuits/ECMO, infection and liver disease.

| **Context** | **Likely issue** | **Treatment distinction** |
|---|---|---|
| Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) | Isolated low platelets ± mucocutaneous bleeding | Steroids/IVIG when indicated; platelet transfusion usually only severe bleeding with adjunctive treatment |
| HIT | Moderate platelet fall with thrombosis | Alternative anticoagulant, avoid platelets routinely |
| TTP | Severe low platelets + MAHA/organ injury | Emergency plasma exchange; avoid prophylactic platelet transfusion |
| DIC | Platelet fall with PT/D-dimer/fibrinogen changes | Treat underlying driver; components for active bleeding |
| Chemotherapy-associated marrow failure | Low production ± neutropenia/anaemia | Infection prevention, thresholds based on bleeding risk; disease treatment |
| CPB-related platelet dysfunction | Early fall, impaired function even at adequate count | Surgical haemostasis, VEM/labs, targeted products |

### Perioperative thresholds should serve a clinical decision

**Most major surgery with bleeding:**

- A platelet count >50 ×10⁹/L is a common pragmatic target; **intracranial/ocular posterior segment/critical-site haemorrhage** often needs a higher target (≈100), and **neuraxial procedures** require a separate risk assessment accounting for trajectory, diagnosis, platelet function and anticoagulants.
- There is no universal safe platelet threshold that covers every neuraxial technique.
- Selected TTP/HIT patients can become worse with indiscriminate platelet transfusion.
- Consider whether low platelets are a marker of underlying disease requiring urgent treatment rather than the problem itself.

### A falling haemoglobin in ICU: separate loss, destruction, dilution and failed production

- A new fall in haemoglobin should prompt a trend-based question: is the patient losing RBCs, destroying RBCs, diluting them, or failing to replace them?
- An isolated Hb value cannot identify the mechanism.
- Recheck the specimen and review transfusion/fluid input, drains, phlebotomy, surgery, CRRT/ECMO, gastrointestinal loss, haemodynamic observations and the blood film.
- Early haemorrhage can coexist with a normal initial Hb, while a sudden Hb fall after large fluid boluses may be dilutional.

| **Pattern** | **Helpful investigations** | **What changes management** |
|---|---|---|
| Occult bleeding | Trend HR/BP/lactate, wound/drains, faeces/urine, imaging for abdominal/retroperitoneal loss, coagulation panel | Find and control bleeding source; correct coagulopathy. RBCs treat delivery, not source. |
| Haemolysis | LDH ↑, unconjugated bilirubin ↑, haptoglobin ↓, reticulocytes often ↑, haemoglobinuria; DAT, blood film, transfusion history | Stop suspect transfusion/causative drug or circuit problem; evaluate mechanical haemolysis, immune haemolysis, TMA or G6PD deficiency. DAT may be negative in nonimmune mechanisms. |
| Inflammation/renal disease/low production | Low or inappropriately normal reticulocytes; ferritin normal/high with reduced iron availability; renal function, B12/folate, medications | Treat sepsis/renal disease and nutritional deficiency where demonstrated; avoid routine ESA/iron simply for an acute inflammatory Hb fall, given delayed effect and potential harm. |
| Bone marrow suppression / infiltration | Other cell lines low, abnormal film or blasts, cytotoxic or viral history | Urgent haematology if severe new pancytopenia, blasts or unexplained leukoerythroblastic picture. |

- Transfuse based on clinical context, not because a diagnostic label was given: for many haemodynamically stable ICU adults, an Hb around 70 g/L is a supported restrictive trigger, but active haemorrhage, acute coronary ischaemia, specific perioperative populations and physiological intolerance require separate judgement.
- Routine erythropoietin for anaemia of critical illness has limited immediate utility and can increase thrombosis; use it only when a defined indication exists.
- The clinical objective is adequate oxygen delivery without avoidable transfusion exposure.

### A falling platelet count: triage for the diagnoses that cannot wait

- Start by confirming genuine thrombocytopenia (film/citrate tube for EDTA clumping) and plotting the timing.
- Immediate post-CPB dilution/consumption, a gradual septic fall, sudden immune drug-induced thrombocytopenia, and a day-5-to-10 HIT pattern suggest very different mechanisms.
- The most dangerous differential is not always the disorder with the lowest platelet count; HIT and TMA can cause organ-threatening thrombosis at moderate counts.

| **Clue** | **Likely diagnosis / investigation** | **Priority action** |
|---|---|---|
| Platelets low, PT/APTT prolonged, D-dimer ↑; fibrinogen may be high early in sepsis | DIC/sepsis-associated coagulopathy; serial FBC/PT/fibrinogen and organ function | Treat cause; replace factors/platelets in active bleeding or procedure, not prophylactically for abnormal tests alone. |
| Platelets ↓ plus MAHA (schistocytes, LDH ↑, low haptoglobin), organ dysfunction; PT/APTT often relatively normal | TMA: TTP (send ADAMTS13 before plasma if possible), HUS or other TMA | Urgent haematology and plasma exchange for suspected TTP; do not await ADAMTS13 if strong suspicion. Avoid routine platelet transfusion in TTP unless life-threatening bleeding. |
| Platelets fall >50%, day 5–10 after heparin or rapid on re-exposure; new thrombosis | HIT: use 4Ts, PF4 immunoassay and functional confirmation | Intermediate/high probability: stop all heparin, start nonheparin anticoagulation if clinically appropriate, investigate thrombosis. Do not give prophylactic platelets routinely. |
| Profound isolated fall after new drug, ± mucosal bleeding | Immune drug-induced thrombocytopenia, ITP; medication review, film and exclusion of TMA/DIC | Stop culprit; ITP treated with steroids/IVIG according to severity; transfused platelets may be rapidly destroyed, reserved for life-threatening bleeding. |
| Gradual fall with neutropenia/anaemia, abnormal film, chemotherapy, viral illness | Marrow suppression / infiltration, hypersplenism | Identify drug/disease and infection risk; targeted transfusion with haematology, not empiric platelets for every mild fall. |

### Apply platelet transfusion thresholds to the actual procedure

- The 2025 AABB/ICTMG international guideline updated several historic thresholds.
- In adults, its recommendations include platelet transfusion below 10 ×10⁹/L for nonbleeding critical-illness consumptive thrombocytopenia, below 10 ×10⁹/L before a compressible-site IJ/femoral CVC, below 20 ×10⁹/L for lumbar puncture, and below 50 ×10⁹/L for major non-neuraxial surgery.
- These are guidance recommendations of differing certainty, not guarantees of procedural safety; ultrasound, operator skill, site compressibility, bleeding phenotype, trajectory and drug-induced platelet dysfunction still matter.
- A diagnostic lumbar puncture threshold is not automatically a safe neuraxial anaesthesia or epidural-catheter threshold: anaesthesia requires separate consensus, context and local policy.
- Critical-site bleeding such as intracranial haemorrhage may call for higher individualized targets, but platelet transfusion is not recommended merely for antiplatelet exposure in a nonoperative intracranial bleed with platelets >100 ×10⁹/L.
- Avoid routine prophylactic platelets in nonthrombocytopenic patients after CPB.

Practical approach for an ICU platelet count of 45 ×10⁹/L:

- If stable with sepsis and no bleeding/procedure, investigate trajectory and cause rather than transfusing automatically.
- For urgent laparotomy with expected bleeding, anticipate the need to achieve a suitable procedural target with the laboratory/surgical team.
- If schistocytes and neurological change are present, urgently assess for TTP before reflex platelet administration.
- If the decline follows heparin plus new DVT, prioritise HIT and thrombosis despite the low count.

items.title: 9. Transfusion reactions: recognising them under general anaesthesia
items.body:
## 9.1 Why a reaction is easily missed in theatre

- The awake patient’s first symptom may be rigors, back pain, itching, chest tightness or dyspnoea.
- **Under GA the earliest signs may instead be unexplained hypotension, rising airway pressure, bronchospasm, hypoxaemia, fever, bleeding/oozing, haemoglobinuria or a rapidly deteriorating arterial trace.** The anaesthetist must recognise an association with transfusion while considering the usual perioperative differentials (haemorrhage, anaesthetic depth, anaphylaxis to a drug, PE, aspiration, acute MI, air embolus).
- Do not wait for the patient to be awake or for laboratory confirmation.

The 2025.1 ANZCA Final SAQ specifically examined **major transfusion reactions during general anaesthesia**. Examiners expected immediate cessation, blood-bank notification, support of ventilation and circulation, an appropriate differential diagnosis and postoperative care. A list of reaction names without the active response is insufficient.

![Transfusion reaction: immediate actions](set2-fig3.png)

Transfusion reaction immediate actions

## 9.2 The universal first five minutes

- **1.** **STOP transfusion immediately.** Clamp the blood line and do not restart the implicated unit. Maintain IV access using fresh giving set with normal saline; stop other nonessential infusions if relevant.
- **2.** **Call for help**, inform surgeon and blood bank/transfusion laboratory, identify the implicated unit(s) and coordinate ICU/haematology support. Check patient identity, blood pack label, compatibility and recent transfusions to detect clerical ABO error. Preserve the pack and giving set for return/testing.
- **3.** **ABCDE:** ensure oxygenation, ventilation, airway pressure and circulation.
  - Give high-flow oxygen if acutely deteriorating, manage shock and bleeding, assess temperature, perfusion, urine colour/output and signs of pulmonary oedema.
  - If anaphylaxis is suspected, **IM/IV adrenaline according to severity and perioperative anaphylaxis protocol**, not antihistamines alone.
- **4.** **Send investigations:** fresh patient group and screen/crossmatch, direct antiglobulin test (DAT), haemolysis screen (plasma free Hb, bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin), CBC, renal function, electrolytes, blood gas/lactate, coagulation and fibrinogen
  - Blood cultures and product culture if sepsis suspected
  - Tryptase for suspected anaphylaxis at protocol times
  - CXR/lung ultrasound/echo and BNP where pulmonary oedema requires distinction.
  - Urine Hb/urinalysis can support haemolysis.
  - Avoid delaying lifesaving treatment for sampling.
- **5.** **Document and monitor** the event, volume/type and timing, treatments and serial observations. Transfer to PACU/HDU/ICU as indicated; communicate to patient and future care providers. Do not continue with additional nonemergency transfusion until blood bank advises on safe products.

## 9.3 Classification by timing and mechanism

| **Reaction** | **Usual timing** | **Mechanism and clinical features** | **Primary response** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Acute haemolytic (AHTR)** | During/within 24 h | ABO incompatibility classically complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis: hypotension, fever, bleeding/DIC, red urine, renal injury | Stop; resuscitate; check identity/DAT/haemolysis; manage shock/DIC/AKI |
| **Febrile non-haemolytic (FNHTR)** | During/within hours | Cytokines/recipient antibodies; fever/rigors; diagnosis of exclusion | Stop and exclude haemolysis/sepsis first; antipyretic; consider later transfusion only with blood-bank agreement |
| **Allergic** | Minutes–hours | Urticaria/pruritus from hypersensitivity | Stop, assess severity; antihistamine if isolated mild symptoms; escalate if airway/circulatory symptoms |
| **Anaphylaxis** | Often immediate | Severe hypersensitivity, occasionally anti-IgA or other mechanisms; bronchospasm, hypotension, angioedema, collapse | Adrenaline/fluids/airway; tryptase, allergy/haematology referral; future washed or selected products when indicated |
| **Bacterial contamination / septic transfusion** | During/within hours | Contaminated component (platelets relatively higher risk); high fever, rigors, shock, DIC | Stop, cultures of patient/product, urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics and sepsis resuscitation |
| **TRALI** | During/≤6 h | Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema via donor antibodies and/or neutrophil/endothelial activation | Stop, oxygen/ventilatory support, notify blood service; diuretics not routine |
| **TACO** | During/≤12 h | Hydrostatic pulmonary oedema from transfusion-related circulatory overload | Stop, sit up, oxygen/CPAP, diurese and reduce fluid; slower/smaller future transfusions |
| **Hypotensive reaction** | During transfusion | Bradykinin-related processes; ACEi and specific filters sometimes implicated | Stop, exclude anaphylaxis/haemolysis/sepsis, manage haemodynamics |
| **Delayed haemolytic** | Days–weeks | Anamnestic RBC alloantibody response; falling Hb, jaundice, positive DAT | Blood-bank antibody work-up, monitor haemolysis, antigen-negative products if future transfusion |
| **Delayed serological** | Days–weeks | New antibody/DAT without clinical haemolysis | Record antibody and provide compatible future products |
| **TA-GVHD** | Usually 1–6 weeks | Viable donor lymphocytes attack recipient tissues | Prevention with irradiated components for selected high-risk patients; high mortality once established |
| **Post-transfusion purpura (PTP)** | ≈5–10 days | Alloimmune severe thrombocytopenia, frequently anti-HPA antibodies | Haematology, IVIG; platelet transfusion often ineffective unless life-threatening bleeding |
| **Transfusion-transmitted infection** | Variable, usually delayed | Viral, bacterial or parasitic transmission | Notify service, infection-specific testing/treatment and traceability |

### The critical clinical comparison: TRALI versus TACO

Both may show **new hypoxaemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates** after blood exposure. The distinction determines treatment but is not always immediately clear; mixed cases exist.

| **Feature** | **TRALI** | **TACO** |
|---|---|---|
| Pathophysiology | Permeability oedema / inflammatory lung injury | Hydrostatic overload / raised filling pressures |
| Time window | During or ≤6 h | During or ≤12 h |
| Blood pressure | Often normotension/hypotension; can vary | Hypertension common; can vary |
| Volume state | No primary evidence overload required | Positive balance, elevated JVP, cardiac/renal disease support diagnosis |
| BNP/NT-proBNP | May be lower but not reliable alone in critical illness | Often elevated; not definitive alone |
| Echocardiography | No obligate LV congestion; concomitant disease possible | Raised filling pressures/HF often supported |
| Treatment | Supportive oxygen, lung-protective ventilation; avoid routine diuretics if not overloaded | Fluid restriction, diuretics, oxygen/CPAP; treat heart/renal failure |

**TRALI types:**

- Type I without an ARDS risk factor; Type II can occur with an ARDS risk factor or mild pre-existing ARDS whose respiratory status had been stable in the 12 h before transfusion.
- Diagnostic definitions require careful temporality and exclusion of other explanations.
- **TACO** is more likely with elderly/infant patients, low body weight, heart/renal impairment, rapid transfusion, high-volume exposure and marked positive fluid balance.
- Prevent with pre-transfusion risk assessment, single-unit prescribing when possible, slower rates, careful balance and diuretics in selected patients.

### Acute haemolysis versus sepsis versus anaphylaxis

- **Acute ABO-incompatible haemolysis** may cause rapid fever, hypotension, haemoglobinuria, back/flank pain (unobtainable under GA), DIC and AKI.
- Cross-check identification immediately; treat perfusion/renal injury, serial coagulation and hyperkalaemia; do not allow a clerical error to be missed.
- **Bacterial sepsis** may cause severe fever/rigors and shock; send cultures from patient and pack and start antibiotics early.
- **Anaphylaxis** often causes bronchospasm, sudden loss of BP, increased airway pressure and urticaria (skin signs may be hidden); treat with adrenaline.
- These can overlap clinically, so stabilise and investigate in parallel.

### Investigating a suspected reaction after the patient has left theatre

- A patient may initially appear stable after a mild unexplained fever during transfusion, then develop jaundice and falling haemoglobin days later.
- Retrieve the original unit identifiers and transfusion timeline, compare pre/post Hb and bilirubin, send DAT and antibody identification, and review prior transfusion/pregnancy and historical antibody records.
- A newly detected clinically significant alloantibody may require antigen-negative RBCs for life even if antibody titres later become undetectable.
- This should be recorded in the hospital/blood service system and in the discharge summary so future emergency transfusion does not reproduce the exposure.

- For suspected **TRALI**, the blood service must investigate donors and potentially quarantine other components: the anaesthetist’s notification has implications beyond this patient.
- For **bacterial contamination**, the service needs both patient and component cultures and may need to recall co-components.
- In **TACO**, document fluid balance, rate, patient weight, cardiac/renal disease and treatment response, then prescribe future transfusions in smaller, slower aliquots with reassessment.
- For **severe allergy/anaphylaxis**, arrange formal follow-up and specify future product modifications rather than simply listing ‘allergic to blood’ without describing the reaction.
- The post-event communication is part of definitive management.

## 9.4 Delayed reactions and longer-term immune consequences

- **Delayed haemolytic reaction** arises when an antibody has waned below detection and reappears after donor antigen exposure.
- Expect unexpectedly low post-transfusion Hb, jaundice, elevated bilirubin/LDH and a newly positive antibody screen/DAT.
- It is particularly important in multi-transfused patients and sickle cell disease; hyperhaemolysis may reduce Hb below the pretransfusion value, making repeat transfusion dangerous except when lifesaving and specialist-directed.

- **Alloimmunisation** complicates future crossmatching and pregnancy.
- **TA-GVHD** presents with fever, rash, diarrhoea, liver dysfunction and marrow aplasia after transfusion; irradiation prevents viable donor lymphocyte engraftment, whereas leukodepletion is insufficient.
- **Transfusion-related immunomodulation (TRIM)** describes potential immunological changes associated with donor exposure, historically linked to postoperative infection or cancer recurrence; contemporary leukoreduction and confounding make causal estimates difficult.
- It is not a separate acute bedside reaction with a definitive diagnostic assay.
- Prevention is principally avoiding unnecessary allogeneic exposure and using appropriately processed products rather than an acute antidote.

### Transfusion governance and consent are also safety interventions

- The transfusion ‘right patient, right product’ check prevents the most catastrophic avoidable acute haemolytic errors.
- Confirm patient identity using independent identifiers and the complete bedside protocol; never assume the pack is correct because the group on a handwritten label looks plausible.
- Document the clinical reason for each component, consent/discussion of expected benefits and risks when feasible, product number, start/end times and physiological response.
- For consent, distinguish donor RBCs from plasma, platelets, specific concentrates, albumin, cell salvage and autologous techniques: patient beliefs and priorities can differ for each.
- If a reaction occurs, retain traceability and communicate with the blood bank to protect **other recipients of components from the same donor**.
- After major haemorrhage, reconcile product use and conduct audit/debrief to identify delays, communication failures or unnecessary products.

### Exam-ready synthesis

- When faced with a bleeding patient, always answer in this order: **recognise severity → call help/activate MHP → control source → maintain oxygen delivery → investigate and correct physiology → use targeted products → monitor complications → plan ICU and prevent recurrence**.
- When faced with a stable anaemic or thrombocytopenic patient, invert the instinct to transfuse: **find the cause → assess clinical risk → treat disease or deficiency → use an evidence-based component threshold if needed → reassess after each intervention**.

items.title: 10. Haemoglobinopathies and haematological malignancy
items.body:
## 10.1 Haemoglobinopathies: why oxygen delivery is not only an Hb number

- Haemoglobin disorders alter globin production or structure, producing chronic anaemia, haemolysis, impaired deformability, organ injury or vaso-occlusion.
- The anaesthetic risk depends on **phenotype, baseline physiology, organ damage and procedure**, not simply whether the patient carries a trait.
- Establish genotype/clinical history, crises, pulmonary hypertension, renal function, transfusion antibodies and baseline Hb before planning surgery.

### Sickle cell disease and trait

- HbS polymerises under deoxygenation, dehydration, acidosis, cold stress and high blood viscosity, causing rigid cells, microvascular occlusion and haemolysis.
- **Sickle cell disease** carries risk of painful vaso-occlusive crisis, **acute chest syndrome**, stroke, AKI, infection (functional asplenia), pulmonary hypertension, cardiac/renal dysfunction and perioperative thrombosis.
- Sickle trait is usually much lower risk but extreme hypoxic/dehydrating stress can matter; do not equate trait with disease.

**Preoperative:**

- Determine HbSS/HbSC/other genotype, crisis burden, previous ACS/stroke, baseline Hb, oxygen requirements, sleep apnoea, pulmonary/cardiac function, renal status, hydroxyurea and transfusion/antibody history.
- Optimise infection and hydration, plan warming, oxygenation, analgesia, thromboprophylaxis and appropriate blood availability.
- In higher-risk procedures selected patients benefit from **preoperative transfusion** (simple or exchange), coordinated with haematology.
- Avoid uncontrolled Hb rise with simple transfusion because hyperviscosity can worsen vaso-occlusion; the goal depends on baseline Hb, genotype and procedure.
- Exchange transfusion can lower HbS fraction without excessive haematocrit.
- Trials show that an aggressive HbS <30% strategy is not universally superior to conservative Hb-based strategies; individualise.

**Intraoperative:**

- Prevent hypoxaemia, hypothermia, acidosis, dehydration, hypotension and venous stasis.
- Use normal oxygenation rather than unneeded prolonged hyperoxia, maintain appropriate euvolaemia, warm the patient and give effective analgesia.
- A tourniquet is a relative risk requiring planning rather than a categorical absolute contraindication in every case.
- **Postoperative:** early lung expansion/mobilisation, incentive spirometry where appropriate, adequate analgesia without excessive hypoventilation, hydration without overload and vigilant observation for acute chest syndrome (new pulmonary infiltrate with respiratory symptoms/fever or hypoxaemia).
- Acute chest syndrome needs oxygen, antibiotics when infection plausible, respiratory support and haematology-directed transfusion/exchange in severe cases.
- Pain crisis must be distinguished from surgical complications, infection and PE.

### Thalassaemia

- Reduced synthesis of α- or β-globin chains causes ineffective erythropoiesis, chronic haemolysis and variable anaemia.
- Trait/minor often causes microcytosis without major anaesthetic implications; **transfusion-dependent thalassaemia major** is a multisystem disease: iron overload may produce dilated/restrictive cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, hepatic dysfunction and endocrine disorders (diabetes/hypogonadism), plus splenomegaly, hypercoagulability and difficult crossmatching.
- Preoperative priorities are echo/ECG, endocrine/metabolic evaluation, transfusion and chelation history, infection status and antibody planning.
- Do not treat microcytosis with iron unless true deficiency is confirmed.
- For major disease, transfusion targets are haematology-specific and not the generic ICU threshold.

### Other haemoglobin disorders

- **HbE and HbC** cause variable microcytosis/haemolysis and may coexist with thalassaemia or HbS.
- **G6PD deficiency** is an enzymopathy rather than a haemoglobinopathy but a useful perioperative differential for drug-/infection-triggered oxidative haemolysis; avoid oxidant drugs according to validated medication lists and monitor haemolysis.
- **Methemoglobinaemia** is a haemoglobin functional disorder caused by oxidant exposure (including some local anaesthetics) or congenital enzymes; suspect cyanosis with saturation gap and confirm by co-oximetry, treating clinically significant cases with methylene blue when appropriate (caution G6PD deficiency).

## 10.2 Haematological malignancies: integrate marrow, treatment and organ effects

- **Leukaemia** may cause anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, DIC (especially APL), hyperviscosity/leukostasis, infection and direct organ infiltration.
- **Lymphoma** can cause mediastinal mass/airway or SVC obstruction, effusions, cytopenias and immunosuppression.
- **Myeloma** may produce renal impairment, hypercalcaemia, lytic bone lesions, anaemia, hyperviscosity and abnormal immunoglobulins.
- **Myeloproliferative neoplasms** can cause simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding (e.g. essential thrombocythaemia with acquired vWF syndrome at extreme counts).
- Management is driven by the specific diagnosis and active complications rather than one generic ‘cancer precautions’ rule.

### Preoperative assessment

- **Disease activity and complications:** CBC/film, clotting/fibrinogen if indicated, infection/neutropenia, renal/liver function, electrolytes and calcium, transfusion needs, bleeding/VTE history, lytic lesions, organomegaly and possible mass effect.
- **Therapy-related injury:** anthracyclines → cardiac dysfunction
  - Bleomycin → pulmonary injury (oxygen should be titrated to physiologic need, not withheld during hypoxaemia)
  - Alkylating agents → lung/marrow injury
  - Immunotherapy → myocarditis/endocrinopathy
  - Steroids → adrenal suppression
  - Stem-cell transplant → infection and transfusion modification requirements.
- **Blood product planning:** alloantibodies, required irradiation/CMV-safe components, platelet refractoriness, anticipated bleeding and avoidance of unnecessary transfusion.
  - A history of stem-cell transplant or purine-analogue therapy may create specific irradiation indications; consult transfusion service rather than assigning identical rules to all cancers.
- **Venous access:** catheter infection/thrombosis and difficult access may influence planning.

### Anaesthetic implications

- Maintain asepsis and avoid avoidable breaks in infection prevention.
- Neutropenia increases infection risk but is not automatically an indication for broad antibiotics unrelated to procedure; apply prophylaxis and infection treatment appropriately.
- Severe thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy can exclude neuraxial techniques until corrected or risk-assessed.
- Mediastinal lymphoma may produce **dynamic airway/cardiovascular collapse on induction or supine positioning:** investigate CT anatomy, positional symptoms, echo/vascular compression and plan spontaneous ventilation/rescue in high-risk cases.
- High tumour burden and cytotoxic treatment can provoke **tumour lysis** (hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, AKI), requiring early recognition, fluid/electrolyte management and haematology involvement.

### Postoperative

- Monitor for haemorrhage, thrombosis, infection, delirium, renal injury and organ toxicity.
- Restart antithrombotic therapy when haemostasis permits, support early mobilisation, coordinate blood product thresholds with the disease team and prevent iatrogenic sampling losses.
- A patient with myeloma and renal injury needs different analgesic/fluids choices from a patient with acute leukaemia and severe coagulopathy.

items.title: 11. Applied cases: from physiology to anaesthetic decisions
items.body:
## Case 1 — Revision hip replacement with Hb 108 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 12 μg/L

**Think:**

- Iron deficiency, not ‘mild anaemia to ignore’.
- Evaluate history of bleeding and cause, discuss GI investigation when indicated, optimise iron (oral if enough time, IV if shorter interval/poor absorption), quantify expected blood loss, consider TXA and cell salvage, have compatible blood available if indicated.
- Avoid prophylactic RBC simply to achieve Hb 130. In the event of ongoing surgical bleeding, transfusion decisions reflect oxygen delivery and haemodynamics, not baseline screening threshold.

## Case 2 — Open vascular repair, rapidly losing 2 L, cold and hypotensive

**Think:**

- Urgent source control, MHP and balanced warm components, not litres of crystalloid; measure iCa, temperature, gas/lactate, fibrinogen, platelets and VEM.
- Consider cell salvage.
- If FIBTEM indicates low fibrin contribution, give cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate guided by dose/response.
- Reassess whether bleeding is surgical or diffuse coagulopathic.
- Do not wait for a textbook haemoglobin of 70 before giving RBCs in exsanguination.

## Case 3 — Septic ICU patient, platelets 62, INR 1.6, fibrinogen 4.2, D-dimer elevated

**Think:**

- Possible early sepsis-associated coagulopathy with fibrinogen preserved as acute-phase reactant, rather than ‘DIC excluded because fibrinogen normal’.
- Trend CBC/PT/fibrinogen, search bleeding/thrombosis and organ injury, treat infection/source, assess prophylactic anticoagulation.
- Avoid FFP to normalise INR without bleeding or procedure.
- Exclude HIT/drug effects if timing fits.

## Case 4 — Difficult extubation after surgery and 2 RBC units: saturation falling, bilateral B-lines

- **Think:** TACO, TRALI, cardiogenic oedema, aspiration, anaphylaxis and negative-pressure oedema. Stop transfusion, assess BP/JVP/balance, echo/CXR, gas, send reaction samples, support oxygenation/CPAP. Diurese if overload; avoid routine diuretic in pure TRALI. Inform blood bank immediately even if another diagnosis is possible.

## Case 5 — Day 7 ICU, platelets 220 to 72 after UFH, new femoral DVT

- **Think:** HIT until assessed, not simply ‘heparin causes thrombocytopenia so stop thromboprophylaxis’. Calculate 4Ts, discontinue all heparin, send PF4/functional testing and start a non-heparin anticoagulant unless bleeding contraindicates. Avoid acute warfarin and prophylactic platelets. Evaluate limb and other thromboses.

## Case 6 — Anticoagulated patient for spinal decompression

**Think:**

- Urgency, indication, last dose, renal clearance, clot versus bleed risk, and exact neuraxial timing/catheter plan.
- Routine perioperative DOAC interruption is **not** identical to ASRA neuraxial guidance.
- Urgent decompression with anticoagulant activity requires senior anaesthesia, surgery and haematology planning, possible drug-specific reversal, and a documented postoperative restart decision.

## Case 7 — Blood-refusing patient for major surgery

**Think:**

- Ask what is accepted: fractions, albumin, autologous salvage, closed circuit, acute normovolaemic haemodilution, erythropoietin, iron and TXA.
- Consent is individual.
- Optimise Hb and haemostasis well ahead, use meticulous surgical control, minimise lab sampling, establish rescue ceiling, involve relevant hospital bloodless-medicine service.
- Respect documented informed decisions.

## Case 8 — Transfusion started 15 minutes ago; severe hypotension, bronchospasm and rash under GA

- **Think:** stop unit, oxygenate/ventilate, give adrenaline for anaphylaxis, treat circulatory collapse and assess haemorrhage/surgical field. Notify blood bank, preserve pack, send tryptase and haemolysis/sepsis samples as appropriate. Monitor in ICU and arrange investigation/future product plan; do not treat with antihistamine alone.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
The evidence below is deliberately tied to **one practical exam decision** per study. Neutral primary findings are not proof of equivalence, and a trial’s population should not be extrapolated to unrelated clinical contexts.

| **Study** | **What was tested and the important result** | **What it changes in practice** |
|---|---|---|
| [TRICC, NEJM 1999](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9971864/) | Restrictive versus liberal RBC triggers in stable critical illness; restrictive was not worse for overall mortality | Avoid automatic Hb 100 g/L in stable ICU patients; exceptions remain |
| [TRISS, NEJM 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25270275/) | Septic shock Hb 70 vs 90 g/L thresholds; comparable mortality with fewer units at 70 | Restrictive strategy usually appropriate in stable septic shock |
| [TRICS III, NEJM 2017](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1711818) | Cardiac surgery restrictive threshold ≈75 g/L noninferior for composite serious outcomes | Cardiac surgery need not routinely maintain Hb 90–100 |
| [MINT, NEJM 2023](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307983) | MI plus anaemia, restrictive versus liberal (<100 g/L) strategy; trend favouring liberal, primary result not statistically definitive | Don’t generalise Hb 70 g/L to active MI without clinical reasoning |
| [PREVENTT, Lancet 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736%2820%2931539-7) | Preop IV iron in anaemic major abdominal surgery improved Hb later but did not reduce transfusion/death primary endpoint | Treat iron deficiency, but don’t promise all IV iron reduces perioperative transfusion |
| [CRASH-2, Lancet 2010](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736%2810%2960835-5) | Early TXA in bleeding trauma reduced death from bleeding; timing crucial | Give within 3 hours when indicated, never replace haemorrhage control |
| [WOMAN, Lancet 2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736%2817%2930638-4) | TXA in postpartum haemorrhage reduced death due to bleeding, especially early | Treat PPH promptly with TXA plus definitive obstetric measures |
| [PROPPR, JAMA 2015](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.12) | 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2 plasma:platelets:RBC trauma; overall mortality difference not significant, improved haemostasis/exsanguination outcomes | Early balanced components; transition to results-guided treatment |
| [POISE-3, NEJM 2022](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171) | TXA in major noncardiac surgery reduced major bleeding, CV safety noninferiority not formally demonstrated | Benefits require balancing thrombosis/stroke uncertainty and procedure |
| [ATACAS, NEJM 2017](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1606424) | TXA in coronary surgery reduced bleeding/reoperation; seizures increased | Dose selection and renal adjustment matter in cardiac surgery |
| [HALT-IT, Lancet 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736%2820%2930848-5) | High-dose TXA in acute GI bleeding did not reduce death due to bleeding; VTE and seizures increased | Do not prescribe TXA for all GI haemorrhage |
| [Villanueva GI bleeding, NEJM 2013](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1211801) | Restrictive RBC strategy in acute upper GI bleeding improved outcomes in a selected cohort | Avoid liberal transfusion once stabilised; adjust for exsanguination/ischaemia |
| [HEMOTION, NEJM 2024](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2404360) | Severe TBI restrictive versus liberal transfusion; primary neurological benefit did not meet significance threshold | TBI transfusion remains individualised, not a universal number |
| [PREPIC2, JAMA 2015](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.3780) | Retrievable IVC filter plus anticoagulation did not reduce symptomatic recurrent PE | Avoid adding routine IVC filter when anticoagulation is possible |
| [PAUSE, JAMA Intern Med 2019](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.2431) | Standardised perioperative DOAC interruption without heparin bridging in AF, low major bleeding/thromboembolism | Routine DOAC bridging unnecessary in many elective patients; not neuraxial rule |
| [BRIDGE, NEJM 2015](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1501035) | In AF on warfarin, no bridging noninferior for thromboembolism and less bleeding | Avoid routine bridging in common AF scenarios; excluded mechanical valves |
| [RE-ALIGN, NEJM 2013](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1300615) | Dabigatran after mechanical valves led to harm versus warfarin | DOACs contraindicated for mechanical prosthetic valves |
| [RECESS, NEJM 2015](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1414217) | RBC storage duration in cardiac surgery not associated with major organ outcome difference | Standard-issue stored RBCs usually acceptable |
| [ABLE, NEJM 2015](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1500704) | Fresher versus standard stored RBCs in critical illness did not improve mortality | Avoid unproven ‘fresh RBC for everyone’ rules |

### Newly incorporated high-yield studies

Monaco et al., NEJM 2025 — ANH before cardiac surgery: 2,010 randomized patients; allogeneic RBC exposure 27.3% with ANH versus 29.2% usual care (P=0.34). This is a useful counterpoint to earlier pooled smaller studies and prevents overclaiming that ANH consistently reduces transfusion.

AABB/ICTMG 2025 international platelet guideline — not a clinical RCT, but a major evidence-synthesis update: more restrictive recommended triggers for selected procedures. Differentiate diagnostic lumbar puncture from epidural/neuraxial anaesthesia.

2025.2 ANZCA examiner report, Question 5 — candidates were required to critically evaluate more than ROTEM alone and explain what each POC test adds to clinical decision-making, including important limitations.

items.body:
## BJA Education — read alongside the chapters

- **1.** [Carroll C, Young F. Intraoperative cell salvage. BJA Education 2021;21:95–101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7892352/). Essential for the circuit, washing, benefits, contamination, oncological/obstetric caveats and safety; directly supports the 2024.2 SAQ.
- **2.** [Point-of-care viscoelastic testing.
  - BJA Education 2022;22:416–423](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9596284/).
  - Learn TEG/ROTEM initiation, kinetics, fibrin/platelet contributions, lysis, practical limitations and assay-specific interpretation.
  - Read with its [published corrigendum](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9947957/).
- **3.** [Regional anaesthesia in patients at risk of bleeding. BJA Education 2021;21:84–94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7892354/). Mechanisms and complications of anticoagulants and the underlying reasoning for neuraxial precautions; **the article’s older timing table must be superseded by 2025 ASRA/local guidance.**
- **4.** [Anaesthetic management of abdominal trauma. BJA Education 2025;25:10–19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11897445/). Damage-control principles, trauma resuscitation and haemorrhage physiology.
- **5.** [Haemostatic agents in the management of obstetric haemorrhage. BJA Education 2024;24:426–432](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.06.005). Fibrinogen, viscoelastic testing and the obstetric bleeding phenotype; detailed PPH is in the obstetrics sets.
